title: Unit 1 – Introduction to Optimal Control and the Dynamic Programming Algorithm
text:
1 Optimal control
Optimality is a useful design principle in many engineering contexts: we size a refrigerator to minimize its energy use, tune an engine to minimize a car’s fuel consumption, shape an aircraft wing to minimize drag, and schedule elevators in a building to minimize passenger waiting time. It is also a principle nature itself seems to follow – many physical laws can be derived from optimality arguments – and, arguably, a principle we apply informally every day whenever we weigh a decision.
Optimal control gives this idea a precise mathematical form for a broad class of problems. These are problems in which optimal decisions, or control actions, are chosen over a period of time so as to minimize a cost that reflects a final objective and, often, intermediate objectives along the way. Optimal control problems arise in the control of physical systems – mechanical, electrical, biological – but also in economics, computer science, game theory, and many other fields. Fig. 1 gives a sense of this breadth, from robotics to logistics to biology.







Fig. 1: Optimal control appears across a wide range of application domains. (Photo credits, Wikimedia Commons: motorcycle racing, “Stepro”, CC BY-SA 4.0 – Hubble Space Telescope in orbit, ESA/Hubble, CC BY 2.0.)




It is worth contrasting optimal control with the more familiar setting of static optimization, which asks for a single optimal decision – for instance, the price of a product, or the slope of a line that best fits a data set. Optimal control differs from static optimization in two important respects. First, it asks for several optimal decisions, made sequentially over time. Second, because the system’s future state cannot be predicted with certainty, a good decision at each point in time should be allowed to depend on the state actually observed at that point, rather than being fixed in advance; that is, the decisions form a control law that can react to disturbances. Given the current state, previous decisions are irrelevant to determining future decisions. This gives optimal control problems a special structure, which the solution methods developed later in the course exploit. Driving a car around a race track, positioning the tip of a robot arm despite external disturbances, or playing chess are all optimal control problems in this sense: not a single choice, but a sequence of choices, each informed by how the situation has evolved.

1.1 Formulating an optimal control problem
Every optimal control problem in this course is built from two ingredients: a dynamic model and a cost function.
The dynamic model specifies the rules of the problem, or the governing equations of the physical system under control. Central to it is the notion of state: a summary of all the information relevant to making future decisions. Control actions are the decisions available to the controller at each point in time; they influence how the state evolves. That evolution may be deterministic, or it may be stochastic, driven by disturbances outside the controller’s influence.
The cost function encapsulates the goals of the problem. It is typically additive over time – a sum of costs incurred at each decision stage – and, by convention, the objective is to minimize it (a reward to be maximized can always be recast as a cost to be minimized by negating it).
The goal of the problem is then to find a control policy minimizing the cost: a policy being a set of functions, one per time instant, mapping the current state to an action. A closely related, and often easier, question is to compute a single optimal path – a sequence of optimal decisions over time – for one specific, given initial condition, rather than a policy valid for every possible initial condition. (In continuous-state settings, introduced shortly, the same idea is usually called an optimal trajectory instead.)


1.2 Classes of optimal control problems and applications
The course begins with problems where the state and action spaces are discrete, and later moves to continuous spaces (\(\mathbb{R}^n\)). Time, throughout the course, is always taken to be discrete; continuous-time decision problems will appear occasionally, but whenever they do, we will convert them into stage-decision or discrete optimization problems rather than treating continuous time directly.
When a discrete- or continuous-state problem is additionally subject to stochastic disturbances, it is called a Markov Decision Process (MDP). This gives four broad classes of problems that recur throughout the course:

The sections that follow make several of these problems concrete, since they will recur as running examples through the course – including settings where uncertainty is explicitly present.

1.2.1 Discrete decision problems
Discrete decision problems and discrete MDPs arise naturally in operational research, management, and finance, where optimal control ideas govern inventory control, the control of a queue, or the control of data and traffic networks. In computer science, closely related problems include finding shortest paths in graphs, scheduling, games, and selection problems, among other applications.
A discrete decision problem is naturally specified by a transition diagram with \(h-1\) decision stages: circles represent the possible states at each stage, arrows represent the actions that lead from a state at one stage to a state at the next, and each arrow carries a cost \(c^k_{i,j}\), the cost of taking action \(j\) from state \(i\) at stage \(k\); at the terminal stage \(h\), each state \(i\) carries a terminal cost \(c^h_i\).






Fig. 2: A transition diagram: circles are states at each stage, arrows are actions leading to the next stage, and each arrow is labeled with its cost.



Working with such diagrams typically raises two challenges, illustrated below with the small example of Fig. 3 (a): (i) determining an optimal path for a given initial state, minimizing the sum of costs incurred at every stage, including the terminal stage (b); and (ii) determining an optimal policy that specifies, for every state, the first decision of the optimal path from that state to the terminal stage (c). Together, these motivate the need for a systematic algorithm, rather than exhaustive enumeration of every path.






Fig. 3: Two characteristic challenges in discrete decision problems: (a) a small example transition diagram; (b) optimal paths for two different initial states; (c) the corresponding optimal policy.



A first running example throughout the course is inventory control: how should a shop manage the supply of a product over time? Overstocking is costly – it ties up physical space and risks technological obsolescence – while understocking undermines sales; the optimal policy must balance the two (Fig. 5 (a), below).
A second is shortest paths in graphs: given a road network, what is the shortest route from one city to another – for instance, from Bucharest to Lugoj in the map below?






ImportantTeaser: Can you find an optimal path planning algorithm in 15 minutes?





Can you find the optimal path from Bucharest to Lugoj yourself? Can you devise an algorithm that would always find optimal paths in graphs, efficiently? As we will see in Unit 3, Dijkstra came up with such an algorithm in just 15 minutes.









Fig. 4: Road map of Romania (Source: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Russell & Norvig, 3rd ed., 2016), used as a running shortest-path example.



A closely related problem is robot path planning: finding the shortest path for a robot moving through a grid from a starting point to a target (Fig. 5 (b)). Discrete decision problems with uncertainty appear naturally in games such as blackjack, where the goal is to play so as to make a profit in expectation (Fig. 5 (c)); and in planning a day at an amusement park, where a visitor uses stochastic models of queueing times at each attraction to decide how to maximize time spent at their favorite attractions (Fig. 5 (d)).






Fig. 5: Four further examples of discrete decision problems: (a) managing the supply of a product in a shop, a natural inventory control problem; (b) shortest-path planning for a robot moving through a grid; (c) games such as blackjack, modeled as a discrete decision problem under uncertainty; (d) planning a day at Efteling under uncertain waiting times.









TipQuick exercise: robot path planning as a road map problem





Can you formulate the robot planning problem in a grid world, as shown in Fig. 5 (b), where cells are either free or obstacles, as a road-map problem? Assume the distance between two horizontally or vertically adjacent cells is \(1\), and the distance between two diagonally adjacent cells is \(\sqrt{2}\).









NoteSolution





View each free cell as a city in a large road map. For two horizontally or vertically adjacent free cells, the distance between them is simply \(1\); for two diagonally adjacent free cells, it is \(\sqrt{2}\). There are no roads from free cells to obstacle cells, nor between obstacle cells (some “cities” are then isolated and can eventually be removed from the road map).





1.2.2 Continuous decision problems
The discrete framework generalizes naturally to problems with a general state and input space, such as \(\mathbb{R}^n\). A continuous decision problem is described by a dynamic model \[x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k,u_k), \qquad k\in\{0,\dots,h-1\},\] where \(x_k\) is the state and \(u_k\) the control input at time \(k\), together with a cost function \[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,u_k) + g_h(x_h).\] As before, there are two related goals: (i) find a policy \(\pi=\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\), with \(u_k=\mu_k(x_k)\), that achieves the minimum cost for every initial condition, or (ii) find a single trajectory \(\{(x_0,u_0),(x_1,u_1),\dots,(x_{h-1},u_{h-1})\}\) achieving the minimum cost for a given initial condition.






Fig. 6: The continuous decision problem generalizes the discrete transition diagram to a general state and input space.



The most prominent application of this framework is digital control: how should one design a digital controller for a physical system, complete with digital-to-analog and analog-to-digital converters, sensors, and actuators? Variants of this problem include cases where the full state is measured versus only a partial output, and cases with or without external disturbances.






Fig. 7: A physical system controlled digitally, with D/A and A/D converters, sensors, and actuators; several variants are possible depending on what is measured and whether disturbances are present.



Several concrete case studies illustrate the range of this framework. Mixing two fluids in minimum time can be posed as a digital control problem in which a camera observes the mixture and an actuator applies one of four possible rotations once every \(h\) seconds.






Fig. 8: Mixing two fluids using camera feedback and a digitally-actuated mixer.



Digitally controlling a unicycle robot – subject to constraints on its speed and rotation rate – to complete a maneuver in minimum time is another instance (Fig. 9 (a), below). So is flying a quadcopter while taking wind-preview information into account (Fig. 9 (b)); moving a satellite between orbits with minimum energy or fuel expenditure – an important concern given the limited fuel satellites carry (Fig. 9 (c)); and moving the tip of a robot arm from one configuration to another in minimum time (Fig. 9 (d)).






Fig. 9: Four further case studies within the digital control framework: (a) a race car cornering, illustrating a vehicle maneuvering under speed and turning-rate constraints in the same spirit as a digitally-controlled unicycle robot (photo: “FIA F1 Austria 2021 Nr. 4 Norris (corner),” Steffen Prößdorf (“Stepro”), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons); (b) quadcopter control that takes wind-preview information into account; (c) minimum-energy orbital transfer for a satellite (photo: Hubble Space Telescope in orbit, ESA/Hubble, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons); (d) a robotic arm performing a task, similar in spirit to minimum-time robot-arm control (photo: “KUKA Industrial Robot Writer,” Mirko Tobias Schäfer, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons).





1.2.3 Continuous-time optimal control problems
Occasionally the underlying physical system is more naturally described in continuous time, via a dynamic model \[\dot{x}(t) = f(t,x(t),u(t)), \qquad x(0)=x_0, \quad t\in[0,h],\] and a cost function \[\int_0^h g(t,x(t),u(t))\,dt + g_h(x(h)),\] with the same two goals as before: find a feedback policy minimizing the cost for every initial condition, or find a single control input minimizing the cost.






Fig. 10: A continuous-time optimal control problem.



Most control-systems applications are naturally posed this way: in traditional process control, they arise in stabilizing and regulating systems such as an inverted pendulum, a mass-spring damper, a double integrator, or a quadcopter; in aerospace, a canonical problem is the minimum-fuel launch of a satellite. As noted above, whenever such problems arise in this course we will approximate them as discrete-time decision or optimal control problems, which is the setting the dynamic programming algorithm developed below is built for.






ImportantTeaser: Find a useful optimal control problem for you!





Some of the problems above – such as finding an optimal policy to visit attractions at Efteling, or taking wind-preview information into account in drone control – were originally proposed by students. Can you creatively think of a problem you would like to solve or work on, that you believe can be cast as an optimal control problem? A couple of suggestions to get you started: how would you schedule your tasks throughout the week, given estimated completion times and estimated rewards for accomplishing each one? Or, what is the optimal driving policy for a solar-powered car trying to drive as far as possible, given estimates of near-future cloud-shadow patterns?





1.2.4 The reinforcement learning setting
A final, important variation on this theme arises when no dynamic model is available at all – only the real system itself, or a simulator that can be run, is accessible. This is the reinforcement learning (RL) setting.






Fig. 11: The reinforcement learning setting: an agent interacts with an environment or simulator, without access to an explicit dynamic model.



Even though no explicit dynamic model is given, a model of the form described above is still implicitly present for analysis purposes; the difference is that it is unknown to the decision-maker. A reward or cost function still encapsulates the goals of the problem, but it is now obtained through the agent’s interaction with the environment rather than computed from a known model. This is, in fact, the key distinguishing feature of reinforcement learning relative to the classical dynamic programming setting introduced above: the transition dynamics are unknown and must be learned from interaction, rather than given. The goal becomes to find a control policy – again, a function from states to actions – that minimizes cost based on data gathered through trial and error.
Two examples illustrate this setting. Learning the optimal policy for a ghost chasing Pacman – deciding, at each step, whether to move up, down, left, or right so as to catch Pacman in minimum time – is a natural discrete RL problem.






Fig. 12: Learning an optimal chasing policy in a Pacman-style game.



Learning to control a robot arm to perform a ball-balancing task is a continuous analogue.






Fig. 13: Learning to control a robot arm for a ball-balancing task. (Figure: MATLAB Reinforcement Learning Toolbox, MathWorks.)









ImportantTeaser: play against the ghost





You can run away from the ghost using the left, right, up, and down arrow keys on your keyboard (click the game board first so that it can receive your key presses). The ghost is following a smart policy, with a model of the environment – can you guess what it is? What if the ghost did not have a model?

text:
2 The dynamic programming algorithm
Having introduced the range of problems optimal control addresses, we turn to the first general-purpose method for solving them: dynamic programming (DP). Dynamic programming allows us to find not just a single optimal path, but entire policies – functions mapping states to actions – which can then be used to control a system in the presence of disturbances. It can also be used to compute optimal paths or trajectories directly, although, as we shall see later in the course, other methods can be more efficient for that narrower task.

2.1 The principle of optimality
Dynamic programming rests on a simple but powerful observation, known as the principle of optimality. Consider a simple example: the shortest route from Eindhoven to Paris happens to pass through Antwerp. The principle of optimality then tells us that the portion of that route from Antwerp to Paris must itself be the shortest route between those two cities – if a shorter route from Antwerp to Paris existed, splicing it in would produce a shorter Eindhoven-to-Paris route, contradicting the optimality of the original route.






Fig. 14: The shortest route from Eindhoven to Paris via Antwerp illustrates the principle of optimality.



Stated more generally, for a discrete optimization problem: the tail of an optimal path is also optimal. Given an optimal path from stage \(0\) to stage \(h\), consider the state at some intermediate stage \(j\) that lies on this optimal path. Then the decisions along the optimal path from stage \(j\) onward to stage \(h\) are themselves optimal for the subproblem that starts at that state at stage \(j\).






Fig. 15: The tail of an optimal path is itself optimal: a formal statement of the principle of optimality.



The principle of optimality is not specific to discrete optimization problems – it applies equally to stage-decision problems and to continuous-time optimal control problems – and it is the foundation on which the dynamic programming algorithm is built.
The argument sketched informally above for the Eindhoven-Antwerp-Paris example is worked out precisely, by contradiction, in the following exercise.






TipExercise: prove the principle of optimality





Consider an optimal path from stage \(0\) to stage \(h\), and an intermediate stage \(j\) that lies on this path. Prove, by contradiction, that the portion of the path from stage \(j\) onward to stage \(h\) is itself optimal for the subproblem that starts at that state at stage \(j\).









NoteSolution





Split the cost of the optimal path into the cost of the portion before stage \(j\) and the cost of the portion from stage \(j\) onward: \[\text{cost} = \text{cost}_{[0,j)} + \text{cost}_{[j,h]}.\]






Fig. 16: Step 1: an optimal path from stage 0 to stage h, split at an intermediate stage j.



Now suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that the portion of this path from stage \(j\) to stage \(h\) is not optimal for the subproblem starting at that state at stage \(j\) – that is, there exists an alternative continuation with strictly smaller cost, \[\underline{\text{cost}}_{[j,h]} < \text{cost}_{[j,h]}.\]






Fig. 17: Step 2: supposing the tail of the path, from stage j onward, is not optimal.



Splicing this better continuation onto the original path’s first portion then produces a path from stage \(0\) to stage \(h\) with strictly smaller total cost, \[\text{cost}_{[0,j)} + \underline{\text{cost}}_{[j,h]} < \text{cost}_{[0,j)} + \text{cost}_{[j,h]},\] contradicting the assumption that the original path was optimal. Hence the tail of an optimal path must itself be optimal.






Fig. 18: Step 3: splicing in the better tail produces a strictly shorter path overall – a contradiction.








2.2 The algorithm
The principle of optimality suggests a natural algorithm for discrete decision problems: rather than search forward from stage \(0\), compute optimal decisions backward from the final stage. Concretely, the dynamic programming algorithm proceeds as follows.

Start at the final decision stage \(h\), and set the cost-to-go at stage \(h\) equal to the terminal cost.
For every state at stage \(k<h\), compute the optimal action by minimizing the sum of the immediate cost and the cost-to-go of the resulting next state; call the minimum value the cost-to-go at stage \(k\) for that state.
Repeat step 2, moving backward through \(k=h-1,h-2,\dots,0\).

Because each state at each stage only ever needs to look one stage ahead (at the cost-to-go values already computed), the entire diagram can be swept once, backward, rather than requiring an exhaustive search over all possible forward paths.


2.3 A worked example
Fig. 19 shows the algorithm being applied stage by stage, backward through a small transition diagram.











(a) Iteration 1 – Stage 3













(b) Iteration 2 – Stage 2













(c) Iteration 3 – Stage 1













(d) Iteration 4 – Stage 0







Fig. 19: The algorithm applied stage by stage, backward through a small transition diagram: first computing the cost-to-go at stage 3 from the terminal cost (a), then propagating it back to stage 2 (b), stage 1 (c), and finally stage 0 (d), completing the backward sweep.



Once the backward sweep is complete, both the optimal policy and the optimal paths can be read directly off the diagram.






Fig. 20: The completed diagram shows the optimal policy (the chosen decision at every state and stage) and allows the optimal path from any initial state to be read off.



While running the algorithm, a decision is made at every state and every stage in order to compute that state’s cost-to-go; this decision is precisely the decision specified by the optimal policy at that state/stage. To obtain the optimal path for a given initial state, simply follow the arrows selected by the policy from that initial state through to the final stage. The cost-to-go computed at stage \(0\) for that initial state coincides exactly with the total cost of the resulting optimal path.






TipQuick exercise: a two-stage recursion by hand





Consider a discrete decision problem with \(h=2\) stages, states \(x_0\in\{1,2\}\) at stage \(0\), states \(x_1\in\{1,2\}\) at stage \(1\), and a single terminal state \(x_2\). The stage costs are: from \(x_0=1\), cost \(3\) to reach \(x_1=1\) and cost \(5\) to reach \(x_1=2\); from \(x_0=2\), cost \(1\) to reach \(x_1=1\) and cost \(4\) to reach \(x_1=2\); from \(x_1=1\), cost \(2\) to reach \(x_2\); from \(x_1=2\), cost \(6\) to reach \(x_2\). The terminal cost is \(g_2(x_2)=0\).

Compute the cost-to-go \(J_1(x_1)\) for each \(x_1\in\{1,2\}\).
Compute the cost-to-go \(J_0(x_0)\) for each \(x_0\in\{1,2\}\), and give the optimal decision at each state.










NoteSolution






At stage \(1\) there is only one available action from each state, so \(J_1(1) = 2\) and \(J_1(2) = 6\).
At stage \(0\): \[J_0(1) = \min\{3+J_1(1),\ 5+J_1(2)\} = \min\{3+2,\ 5+6\} = \min\{5,11\} = 5,\] achieved by moving to \(x_1=1\); and \[J_0(2) = \min\{1+J_1(1),\ 4+J_1(2)\} = \min\{1+2,\ 4+6\} = \min\{3,10\} = 3,\] also achieved by moving to \(x_1=1\). So the optimal policy sends both \(x_0=1\) and \(x_0=2\) to \(x_1=1\) at stage \(0\), and from \(x_1=1\) (the only option) to \(x_2\) at stage \(1\). The optimal cost-to-go from \(x_0=1\) is \(5\); from \(x_0=2\) it is \(3\).










NotePython companion





As a companion to solving the recursion above by hand, here is the same backward recursion implemented directly in Python. Unlike the surrounding text, this code cell is live: Quarto executes it when the document is rendered (given a Python/Jupyter environment), and the output shown below the cell is produced by actually running the code, not typed in by hand. The parameters describing the problem instance are kept in a clearly marked block at the top, separate from the recursion logic: to try a different transition diagram, edit only that block (add or remove stages, states, or actions) and re-render – the recursion below adapts automatically, with no other changes needed.

# --- parameters: edit these to try a different problem ---------------------
# cost[k] maps each state at stage k to a dict {next_state: arc_cost},
# describing the actions available from that state. Add/remove stages,
# states, or actions freely -- the recursion below adapts automatically.
cost = {
    0: {1: {1: 3, 2: 5}, 2: {1: 1, 2: 4}},
    1: {1: {"end": 2}, 2: {"end": 6}},
}
# terminal_cost maps each state at the final stage to its terminal cost g_h
terminal_cost = {"end": 0}
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

# --- backward recursion (no need to edit below this line) ------------------
stages = sorted(cost.keys())      # decision stages, e.g. [0, 1, ...]
h = stages[-1] + 1                 # terminal stage index

J = {h: terminal_cost}             # cost-to-go, keyed by stage then state
policy = {}                        # optimal next state, keyed by stage then state

for k in reversed(stages):
    J[k], policy[k] = {}, {}
    for state, actions in cost[k].items():
        best_next, arc_cost = min(
            actions.items(), key=lambda item: item[1] + J[k + 1][item[0]]
        )
        J[k][state] = arc_cost + J[k + 1][best_next]
        policy[k][state] = best_next

for k in stages:
    for state in sorted(J[k], key=str):
        print(f"stage {k}, state {state}: J = {J[k][state]}, "
              f"optimal next state = {policy[k][state]}")

stage 0, state 1: J = 5, optimal next state = 1
stage 0, state 2: J = 3, optimal next state = 1
stage 1, state 1: J = 2, optimal next state = end
stage 1, state 2: J = 6, optimal next state = end


The printed values match the by-hand computation above exactly: \(J_1(1)=2\), \(J_1(2)=6\), \(J_0(1)=5\), \(J_0(2)=3\), with both \(x_0=1\) and \(x_0=2\) optimally routed through \(x_1=1\). Because the recursion above only ever reads the cost and terminal_cost dictionaries – it never hardcodes the number of stages or states – you can extend the parameters block with a third stage, extra states, or different costs, and the same code will compute the correct backward recursion for that new problem.





2.4 Non-uniqueness
It can happen that, at some state and stage, more than one action achieves the same minimum cost-to-go. When this occurs, any of the tied options may be selected; the algorithm simply picks one of them (arbitrarily, or by convention) and proceeds. The result is a single optimal policy, even though, in general, several different optimal policies may exist – all of them achieving the same optimal cost-to-go, but potentially prescribing different actions at the states and stages where a tie occurred.






Fig. 21: An example of non-uniqueness: more than one action achieves the same cost-to-go at a given state and stage.









TipQuick exercise: counting optimal policies under ties






Suppose that, while running the DP algorithm, a tie in the cost-to-go between two actions occurs at \(r\) different state-stage pairs (possibly at different stages). How many optimal policies does the problem have?
Suppose instead that ties occur at only two state-stage pairs, with \(3\) optimal actions available at the first and \(4\) optimal actions available at the second. How many optimal policies are there in total?










NoteSolution






At each of the \(r\) tied state-stage pairs, either of the two optimal actions can be selected independently of the choices made at the other tied pairs, and every such combination yields a distinct optimal policy (all achieving the same optimal cost). There are therefore \(2^r\) optimal policies.
By the same reasoning, the choice made at the first state-stage pair (among \(3\) optimal actions) is independent of the choice made at the second (among \(4\) optimal actions), so the total number of optimal policies is \(3 \times 4 = 12\).






2.5 Inventory control, revisited
We now return to the inventory control problem introduced earlier and formulate it precisely, as a running example for the dynamic programming algorithm. The problem is to control the supply of a single product over time. The dynamic model is \[x_{k+1} = \max\{x_k+u_k-d_k,0\}, \qquad u_k \in \{0,1,\dots,N-x_k\},\] where \(x_k\) is the number of items in stock, \(u_k\) the supply ordered at stage \(k\), \(d_k\) the demand at stage \(k\), and \(N\) the storage capacity. The cost function is \[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,u_k) + g_h(x_h),\] where the stage cost is \[g_k(x_k,u_k) = \big(c_1(x_k) + c\,u_k + c_{tr}\lVert u_k\rVert_0\big) - p\min\{d_k,x_k+u_k\},\] with \(\lVert u_k\rVert_0\) equal to \(0\) if \(u_k=0\) and \(1\) otherwise, \(g_h\) the terminal cost, \(p\) the selling price per item, \(c\) the purchase price per item, \(c_{tr}\) the (fixed, per-order) transportation price, and \(c_1\) the storage cost.
The corresponding transition diagram represents, at each stage, the possible numbers of items in stock as states, with the chosen supplies determining the transitions between them.






Fig. 22: Transition diagram for the inventory control problem: circles at each stage indicate the number of items in stock, and supplies determine the transitions.



To make this concrete, consider a numerical instance with \(h=4\) stages and capacity \(N=4\), demand \(d_0=d_1=2\), \(d_2=d_3=1\), selling price \(p=10\), purchase price \(c=5\), transportation price \(c_{tr}=0.5\), storage cost \(c_1(i)=0.2i\) for \(i\in\{0,\dots,N\}\), and terminal cost \(g_4(i)=-r_{i+1}\) for \(i\in\{0,\dots,4\}\), with \(r=[0\ 4.8\ 9.6\ 14.4\ 19.2]\). Applying the backward recursion to this instance proceeds exactly as in the abstract worked example above.






Fig. 23: Several iterations of the backward recursion applied to the numerical inventory example.



Once the recursion is complete, the resulting policy and the optimal path for each possible initial state can be read off the diagram, exactly as described above.






Fig. 24: The final policy and optimal path for the inventory control example.



A full Python implementation of this example – reproducing the same numbers, including the open-loop/closed-loop figures further below in this section – is available in code/unit1/inventory_control.py, built on top of the general solver in code/unit1/dp.py; the original annotated notebooks are also included there (A_1_inventorycontrol.ipynb, A_1_dp.ipynb). These are ordinary Python files meant to be downloaded and run locally, rather than live in-browser snippets, since the general solver is a bit more involved than the short examples embedded directly in this page.


2.6 Coping with uncertainty






NoteOptional: coping with uncertainty





The dynamic programming algorithm developed above assumes the demand sequence \(d_k\) is known in advance. In practice, of course, it is not: the real value of \(d_k\) only becomes known once stage \(k\) is reached. This section uses the inventory control example to illustrate the difference between planning that ignores this uncertainty and planning that exploits it – a distinction that motivates the extension to stochastic dynamic programming taken up in the next unit.
Consider again the inventory control example, and suppose the plan was computed assuming an expected demand of \(d_2=1\) at stage \(2\), but the realized demand turns out to be \(d_2=2\) instead.






Fig. 25: The inventory control example, used to illustrate open-loop versus closed-loop decision-making under uncertainty.



Because the realized demand differs from what was planned for, the state actually reached at stage \(3\) is \(x_3=0\) rather than the \(x_3=1\) that had been anticipated. Two ways of proceeding from here are worth distinguishing:

Open loop: ignore the discrepancy and blindly apply the action \(u_3=0\) that had originally been planned for the anticipated state.
Closed loop: instead, use the dynamic programming policy computed for the state actually observed, \(x_3=0\), which prescribes \(u_3=1\).

The two choices lead to different realized costs. For the open-loop choice, \[g_0(0,4)+g_1(2,0)+g_2(0,2)+g_3(0,0)+g_4(0) = 0.5 - 19.6 + (-9.5) + 0 + 0 = -28.6,\] whereas for the closed-loop choice, \[g_0(0,4)+g_1(2,0)+g_2(0,2)+g_3(0,1)+g_4(0) = 0.5 - 19.6 + (-9.5) + (-4.5) + 0 = -33.1.\] The closed-loop cost is lower (recall costs here are net of revenue, so more negative is better): by reacting to the observed state rather than following a fixed plan, the closed-loop policy recovers some of the value lost to the unexpected demand.
The same comparison can be made in expectation. If \(\text{Prob}[d_2=1]=0.5\) and \(\text{Prob}[d_2=2]=0.5\), and the open-loop and closed-loop costs when \(d_2=1\) both equal \(-28.4\) (the case that matches what was planned for), then the expected costs are \[\text{Open loop:} \quad 0.5\times(-28.4) + 0.5\times(-28.6) = -28.5,\] \[\text{Closed loop:} \quad 0.5\times(-28.4) + 0.5\times(-33.1) = -30.75.\] The closed-loop policy achieves a strictly lower expected cost, since it is able to adapt its later decisions to the disturbance actually realized, rather than committing to a fixed sequence of actions in advance. Making this idea precise – computing policies that directly minimize expected cost under a known probability distribution over disturbances – is exactly the subject of Unit 2, stochastic dynamic programming.






TipQuick exercise: open loop vs. closed loop without disturbances





True or false: if a discrete decision problem has no disturbances at all (the dynamic model \(x_{k+1}=f_k(x_k,u_k)\) is fully deterministic), then the open-loop and closed-loop strategies always achieve exactly the same cost, for any initial state. Justify your answer.









NoteSolution





True. The gap between open-loop and closed-loop only arises because a disturbance can push the realized state away from the state that was anticipated when the plan was made, so that re-optimizing from the actual state (closed loop) can differ from – and do better than – blindly following the original plan (open loop). Without disturbances, the state at every stage evolves exactly as predicted when the open-loop plan was computed, so the “actual” state the closed-loop policy would react to is, at every stage, precisely the state the open-loop plan already assumed. The closed-loop policy therefore prescribes the same action as the open-loop plan at every stage, the two strategies coincide exactly, and so do their costs.

title: Unit 1 – Introduction to Optimal Control and the Dynamic Programming Algorithm
text:
3 Dynamic programming equations

3.1 A more general formalism
The transition-diagram picture used so far is intuitive, but it is useful to also express the dynamic programming algorithm in a more compact, purely algebraic formalism – equivalent to the one above, but easier to generalize to the settings encountered later in the course (stochastic disturbances, continuous state spaces, and so on).
As before, the dynamic model is \(x_{k+1}=f_k(x_k,u_k)\) for \(k\in\{0,\dots,h-1\}\), and the cost is \(\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,u_k)+g_h(x_h)\).






Fig. 26: The general discrete decision problem, restated in the compact formalism used for the dynamic programming equations.



Concretely, at each stage \(k\) the state takes values in a finite set, \(x_0\in\{1,\dots,n_0\}\), \(x_1\in\{1,\dots,n_1\}\), …, \(x_h\in\{1,\dots,n_h\}\), and the action available at state \(x_k\) takes values in a set that may depend on the state, \(u_0\in\{1,\dots,m_{0,x_0}\}\), \(u_1\in\{1,\dots,m_{1,x_1}\}\), …. The stage costs are simply the arrow costs from before, relabeled as \(g_0(x_0,u_0)=c^0_{x_0,u_0}\), \(g_1(x_1,u_1)=c^1_{x_1,u_1}\), …, and the terminal cost as \(g_h(x_h)=c^h_{x_h}\).






TipQuick exercise: writing down \(f_k\), \(g_k\), and \(g_h\) for a small example





Consider the small transition diagram at the top of Fig. 21 above: one state at stage \(0\), two states at stage \(1\), and two (terminal) states at stage \(2\) (\(h=2\)). Write down the dynamics \(f_k\), the stage costs \(g_k\), and the terminal cost \(g_h\) for this problem, in the general formalism introduced above.









NoteSolution





Label actions by the state they lead to, so that \(f_k(x_k,u_k)=u_k\) at every stage. There is a single state at stage \(0\), \(x_0=1\), with two available actions: \[g_0(1,1) = 3, \qquad g_0(1,2) = 2,\] matching the two arrows leaving state \(1\) in the diagram (to state \(1\) and to state \(2\) at stage \(1\), respectively).
At stage \(1\) there are two states, \(x_1\in\{1,2\}\), each with two available actions: \[g_1(1,1) = 3, \qquad g_1(1,2) = 3, \qquad g_1(2,1) = 1, \qquad g_1(2,2) = 3,\] again matching the four arrows from stage \(1\) to stage \(2\) in the diagram.
Finally, the terminal cost at stage \(h=2\) is \[g_2(1) = 2, \qquad g_2(2) = 0.\]
As a check, the two optimal paths shown in Fig. 21 both have total cost \(5\): \(g_0(1,2)+g_1(2,2)+g_2(2) = 2+3+0=5\), and \(g_0(1,2)+g_1(2,1)+g_2(1) = 2+1+2=5\).





3.2 The dynamic programming equations
In this formalism, the dynamic programming algorithm becomes a compact pair of recursive equations. Denoting by \(U_k(i)\) the set of actions available at state \(i\) and stage \(k\), we initialize \[J_h(i) = g_h(i)\] for every state \(i\), and then, for each stage starting from the last and moving backward, compute \[
J_k(i) = \min_{j\in U_k(i)} \; g_k(i,j) + J_{k+1}(j),
\] together with the corresponding minimizer \(\mu_k(i)=j^\star\). The function \(J_k\) is exactly the cost-to-go at stage \(k\) from the diagram picture above, and \(\mu_k\) is exactly the optimal policy: at each state \(i\) and stage \(k\), the policy prescribes the action \(\mu_k(i)\) that achieves the minimum in the recursion. These two equations – the initialization at the terminal stage and the backward recursion – are what we will refer to as the dynamic programming equations throughout the rest of the course; the same two equations, suitably adapted, will reappear for stochastic, continuous-state, and infinite-horizon problems.
The dynamic programming equations express a trade-off often encountered in real life: should a decision be made to maximize immediate reward (the function \(g_k\)), or should it instead favor the long-run reward (the function \(J_{k+1}\))? The dynamic programming equations naturally strike this balance, by adding the two together and optimizing their sum at every stage, rather than treating either one in isolation.






TipQuick exercise: counting the data in a problem instance





In the formalism above, suppose a problem has \(h=5\) stages, every state space has exactly \(n_k=4\) states, and every state has exactly \(3\) actions available. How many stage-cost values \(c^k_{i,j}\) need to be specified in total to fully describe the problem (excluding the terminal costs)?









NoteSolution





At each of the \(k\in\{0,\dots,4\}\) stages (that is, \(h=5\) stages), each of the \(4\) states has \(3\) available actions, so \(4\times 3 = 12\) cost values are needed per stage. Across \(5\) stages, that is \(5\times 12 = 60\) stage-cost values \(c^k_{i,j}\) in total (plus \(4\) terminal costs \(c^h_i\), one per state at the terminal stage, which are not counted in the question).









TipQuick exercise: computing costs-to-go for the same example





Using the functions \(f_k\), \(g_k\), and \(g_h\) found in the earlier exercise for the transition diagram on top of Fig. 21, compute the cost-to-go \(J_k(i)\) at every state and stage, and the resulting optimal policy, using the dynamic programming equations.









NoteSolution





At the terminal stage, \[J_2(1) = g_2(1) = 2, \qquad J_2(2) = g_2(2) = 0.\]
At stage \(1\): \[J_1(1) = \min\{g_1(1,1)+J_2(1),\ g_1(1,2)+J_2(2)\} = \min\{3+2,\ 3+0\} = 3,\] achieved uniquely by \(\mu_1(1)=2\); and \[J_1(2) = \min\{g_1(2,1)+J_2(1),\ g_1(2,2)+J_2(2)\} = \min\{1+2,\ 3+0\} = 3,\] achieved by both \(\mu_1(2)=1\) and \(\mu_1(2)=2\) – exactly the tie already highlighted in Fig. 21.
At stage \(0\): \[J_0(1) = \min\{g_0(1,1)+J_1(1),\ g_0(1,2)+J_1(2)\} = \min\{3+3,\ 2+3\} = 5,\] achieved uniquely by \(\mu_0(1)=2\).
The optimal cost starting from \(x_0=1\) is therefore \(J_0(1)=5\), obtained by first moving to state \(2\) at stage \(1\), and then, because of the tie at that state, either to state \(2\) or to state \(1\) at the terminal stage – matching the two optimal paths and two optimal policies shown in Fig. 21.





3.3 Historical note
Dynamic programming was proposed in the 1940s by the American mathematician Richard E. Bellman, whose name is now attached to the recursive equations above (the “Bellman equations”) and to the principle of optimality itself.






Fig. 27: Richard E. Bellman (1920-1984), who proposed dynamic programming in the 1940s.




Photo: via Wikipedia.

Bellman later reflected on the choice to pursue this line of research in these terms:

“I was intrigued by dynamic programming. It was clear to me that there was a good deal of good analysis there. Furthermore, I could see many applications. It was a clear choice. I could either be a traditional intellectual, or a modern intellectual using the results of my research for the problems of contemporary society.”
– R. E. Bellman (1920-1984)

title: Unit 1 – Introduction to Optimal Control and the Dynamic Programming Algorithm
text:
4 Summary
This unit introduced optimal control as the problem of determining several optimal decisions over time, each allowed to depend on the state of the system, in contrast with static optimization’s single decision. We distinguished three broad classes of optimal control problems – discrete optimization, stage-decision, and continuous-time control – and surveyed a wide range of applications across engineering, operations research, computer science, and reinforcement learning. We then introduced the dynamic programming algorithm: a backward recursion, grounded in the principle of optimality, that computes optimal decisions stage by stage and yields both the optimal policy and the optimal cost-to-go at every state and stage. The same recursion, expressed compactly as the dynamic programming equations, will be extended throughout the rest of the course to stochastic, continuous, and infinite-horizon settings.






ImportantTeaser: Room for improvement





While we have seen, in this unit, many optimal control problems that have already been solved – and whose optimal solutions we use nowadays (games, inventory control, optimal robot motion, and so on) – there remains a large number of problems for which, sometimes surprisingly, the optimal policy is not yet used in practice. For instance, have you ever thought that the order in which we draw the individual strokes of our handwritten letters could be optimized to write faster? title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
3 Stochastic formulation
Dynamic model \(\quad x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k,u_k,w_k) \qquad w_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n_w} \text{ (stochastic disturbances)}\)
Cost \(\quad \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,u_k,w_k) + g_h(x_h)\)
Find a policy \(\pi=\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\), \(u_k=\mu_k(x_k)\), that minimizes
\[J_\pi(x_0) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,\mu_k(x_k),w_k) + g_h(x_h)\Big]\]
We assume that the stochastic disturbances have zero mean and are statistically independent (white).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
4 Stochastic dynamic programming algorithm

Start with \(J_h(x_h)=g_h(x_h)\) for every \(x_h \in X_h\) and for each decision stage, starting at the last and moving backwards, \(k \in \{h-1,h-2,\dots,0\}\), compute \(\mu_k\) and \(J_k\) from
\[J_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k \in U_k(x_k)} \mathbb{E}_{w_k}\big[g_k(x_k,u_k,w_k) + J_{k+1}(f_k(x_k,u_k,w_k))\big] \quad \text{(DP equation)}\]
and
\[\mu_k(x_k) = u_k\]
where \(u_k\) is the minimizer in the DP equation. Then \(\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\) is an optimal policy.

To be more precise we can write the right hand side of the DP equation as
\[\mathbb{E}_{w_k}\big[g_k(x_k,u_k,w_k)+J_{k+1}(f_k(x_k,u_k,w_k))\,|\,x_k\big]\]
which reinforces the fact that \(x_k\) is assumed to be constant when computing the expected value and evaluating the minimum.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
5 Linear quadratic control
Dynamic model \(\quad x_{k+1}=A_kx_k+B_ku_k+w_k \qquad k\in\{0,\dots,h-1\} \qquad \mathbb{E}[w_k]=0 \text{ and white}\)
Cost function \(\quad \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} \begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q_k & S_k \\ S_k^\intercal & R_k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k \\ u_k\end{bmatrix} + x_h^\intercal Q_h x_h\)
Find a policy \(\pi=\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\), \(u_k=\mu_k(x_k)\), that minimizes
\[\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} \begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q_k & S_k \\ S_k^\intercal & R_k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k \\ u_k\end{bmatrix} + x_h^\intercal Q_h x_h\Big]\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
6 Optimal policy

Theorem. The optimal policy for the linear quadratic control problem is
\[u_k = K_kx_k \qquad k \in \{0,\dots,h-1\}\]
where
\[K_k = -\big(B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k+R_k\big)^{-1}\big(S_k^\intercal+B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k\big)\]
\[P_k = A_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k+Q_k - \big(S_k+A_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k\big)\big(B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k+R_k\big)^{-1}\big(S_k^\intercal+B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k\big)\]
\[P_h=Q_h \qquad k\in\{h-1,\dots,0\} \qquad \text{(Riccati iterations)}\]
and the resulting expected cost is given by
\[J_0(x_0) = x_0^\intercal P_0 x_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{h-1} \text{trace}\big(P_{k+1}\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal]\big)\]

Proof: see Appendix A.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
7 Discussion

The optimal policy is exactly the same as in the case \(w_k=0\).
Recall the approaches to cope with stochastic disturbances: open loop (use the decisions of the optimal path), closed-loop (use the policy from deterministic DP), closed-loop (use the policy from stochastic DP).
The result of the previous slide says that when the dynamic model is linear and the cost is quadratic, the following holds: these three approaches coincide.
When this happens we say that we have certainty equivalence.
The cost increases when we consider disturbances (intuitive!)

\[J_0(x_0) = \underbrace{x_0^\intercal P_0 x_0}_{\text{cost without disturbances}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\text{trace}(P_{k+1}\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal])}_{\text{additional cost}}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
8 Discussion

The result carries over if we consider an infinite horizon cost, under the same assumptions that we have considered in the deterministic case

\[\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^\infty x_k^\intercal Qx_k+2x_k^\intercal Su_k+u_k^\intercal Ru_k\Big]\]
(optimal policy \(u_k=\bar Kx_k\), \(\bar K=-(B^\intercal \bar P B+R)^{-1}(S^\intercal+B^\intercal \bar P A)\) where \(\bar P\) satisfies the algebraic Riccati equation).

However, now we need the extra assumption that the cost is bounded. If this is the case (e.g. if \(w_\ell=0\), \(\ell>L>0\)) it is given by

\[x_0^\intercal \bar P x_0 + \sum_{k=0}^\infty \text{trace}(\bar P \mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal])\]

If the cost is not bounded we can consider an alternative (average) cost

\[\lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T}\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{T-1} x_k^\intercal Qx_k+2x_k^\intercal Su_k+u_k^\intercal Ru_k\Big]\]
which converges to \(\text{trace}(\bar P W)\), assuming \(W=\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal]\ \forall k\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
9 Example
Double integrator considered previously
\[x_{k+1} = \begin{bmatrix}1&\tau\\0&1\end{bmatrix}x_k + \begin{bmatrix}\frac{\tau^2}{2}\\\tau\end{bmatrix}u_k \qquad \tau=0.2\]
\[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}(x_k^\intercal Qx_k+u_k^\intercal Ru_k)+x_h^\intercal Q_hx_h \qquad Q=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} \qquad R=1\]
Optimal policy \(u_k=Kx_k\), \(k\geq 0\) \(\qquad K=\begin{bmatrix}-0.8412 & -1.54\end{bmatrix}\)
Optimal control input and states for \(x_0=[y_0\ \ v_0]^\intercal=[1\ \ 0]^\intercal\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
10 Effects of disturbances
Consider now a disturbance at time 2 sec (\(k=10\))
\[x_{k+1} = \begin{bmatrix}1&\tau\\0&1\end{bmatrix}x_k + \begin{bmatrix}\frac{\tau^2}{2}\\\tau\end{bmatrix}u_k+w_k \qquad w_k = \begin{cases}\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}, & \text{if } k\in\mathbb{N}_0\setminus\{10\} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0\\a\end{bmatrix}, & \text{if } k=10\end{cases}\]
where \(a\) is a uniform random variable in the interval \([-0.5\ \ 0.5]\).
Open loop (top row) / Closed loop (bottom row)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
11 Computing the expected cost
We can compute the expected cost based on the expression
\[x_0^\intercal \bar P x_0+\sum_{k=0}^\infty \text{trace}\big(\bar P\,\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal]\big) = x_0^\intercal \bar P x_0+\text{trace}\Big(\bar P\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&\mathbb{E}[a^2]\end{bmatrix}\Big)\]
where \(\bar P\) is the solution to the algebraic Riccati equation which for the considered parameters is
\[\bar P = \begin{bmatrix}9.1890 & 5.0249\\5.0249 & 9.2324\end{bmatrix}\]
and we used the fact that \(w_k=\begin{cases}\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}, & \text{if } k\in\mathbb{N}_0\setminus\{10\} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0\\a\end{bmatrix}, & \text{if } k=10\end{cases}\)
Since \(x_0=[0\ \ 1]^\intercal\) and \(\mathbb{E}[a^2]=\int_{-0.5}^{0.5} t^2dt = 1/12\) we obtain the cost \(9.95\).

text:

average cost of 5000 simulations: \(9.95\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
14 Problem formulation
Dynamic model \(\quad x_{k+1}=f_k(x_k,u_k,w_k) \qquad\) (stochastic disturbances, initial state unknown)
Cost \(\quad \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,u_k,w_k)+g_h(x_h)\)
Output \(\quad y_k=h_k(x_k,u_{k-1},n_k) \qquad\) (noise)
Information set \(\quad I_0=(y_0), \quad I_k=(y_0,y_1,\dots,y_k,u_0,u_1,\dots,u_{k-1}), \quad k\geq 1\)
Find a policy \(\pi=\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\), \(u_k=\mu_k(I_k)\), which minimizes
\[J_\pi = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,\mu_k(I_k),w_k) + g_h(x_h)\Big]\]
We assume that the initial state, the stochastic disturbances and the output noise have zero mean, are statistically independent and have a known probability distribution.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
15 First approach
We can reformulate a partial information optimal control problem as a standard full information optimal control problem by considering the state to be the information set. The problem is that the state space dimension increases exponentially.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
16 Second approach
It is possible to show that the knowledge of the probability distribution of the state given the information obtained so far, denoted by \(P_{x_k|I_k}\), is sufficient to determine optimal decisions.
\[u_k = \mu_k(P_{x_k|I_k})\]





The state space dimension is now fixed. However, it is typically not easy to store \(P_{x_k|I_k}\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
17 Problem formulation
Dynamic model \(\quad x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k+w_k \qquad k\in\{0,\dots,h-1\} \qquad\) (zero mean \(\mathbb{E}[w_k]=0\) and independent)
Cost function \(\quad \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q&S\\S^\intercal&R\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k\\u_k\end{bmatrix}+x_h^\intercal Q_hx_h\)
Output equation \(\quad y_k=Cx_k+n_k \qquad\) (noise: zero mean and independent)
Information set \(\quad I_k=(y_0,y_1,\dots,y_k,u_0,u_1,\dots,u_{k-1})\)
Find a policy \(\pi=\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\), \(u_k=\mu_k(I_k)\), which minimizes
\[\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q&S\\S^\intercal&R\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k\\u_k\end{bmatrix}+x_h^\intercal Q_hx_h\Big]\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
18 Problem formulation

The initial condition follows a Gaussian (or Normal) distribution with mean \(\bar x_0\) and covariance \(\bar\Phi_0=\mathbb{E}[(x_0-\bar x_0)(x_0-\bar x_0)^\intercal]\), denoted \(x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar x_0,\bar\Phi_0)\)






\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^k\det(\Sigma)}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-\bar x_0)^\intercal \bar\Phi_0^{-1}(x-\bar x_0)} \qquad \text{Prob}[x_0\in A] = \int_A f(x)dx\]
Example: \(x_0=[1\ \ 2]^\intercal\), \(\bar\Phi_0=\begin{bmatrix}2&0.5\\0.5&2\end{bmatrix}\)

The noise variables \(n_k\) are independent random variables following a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and covariance \(V=\mathbb{E}[n_kn_k^\intercal]\), i.e., \(n_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,V)\).
The disturbances variables \(w_k\) are independent random variables following a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and covariance \(W=\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal]\), i.e., \(w_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,W)\).
For simplicity we consider time-invariant matrices for the model and cost.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
19 Outline

Stochastic dynamic programming and linear quadratic control
Output feedback linear quadratic control

Separation principle
Kalman filter
LQG design

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
20 General solution structure
From our general discussion, we know that we can first estimate \(P_{x_k|I_k}\) and then make decisions (control)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
21 Solution
It turns out that (see Appendix D):

\(P_{x_k|I_k}\) is Gaussian, characterized by mean \(\hat x_{k|k}\) and covariance \(\Phi_{k|k}=\mathbb{E}[(x_k-\hat x_{k|k})(x_k-\hat x_{k|k})^\intercal|I_k]\) which can be obtained by the Kalman filter.
The decision maker is the linear quadratic controller \(u_k=K_k\hat x_{k|k}\) with the state replaced by the estimate where the gains are obtained from the Riccati equations.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
22 Discussion

This is one of the most beautiful & most useful results in control theory! The controller is called linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) compensator.
Separation principle: LQG = LQR + LQE.*

As we have seen the LQR is the optimal controller when full state feedback is available.
For a linear system with the dynamic and output models above and known input, the Kalman filter can be shown to be the optimal estimator in the sense that for \(F\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times n}\) and output \(z_k=Fx_k\), the estimate \(\hat z_k=F\hat x_{k|k}\) minimises, for every \(k\), the cost \(\mathbb{E}[(z_k-\hat z_k)^2|I_k]\).
The LQG is the optimal controller among all the possible controllers (including non-linear controllers) when the noise, disturbances and initial conditions are Gaussian (non-Gaussian noise mentioned later).

Resulting optimal cost is (see appendix D):

\[J_0(I_0) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[x_0^\intercal P_0x_0|I_0]}_{\text{full state \& no disturbances}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\text{trace}(P_{k+1}\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal])}_{\text{additional cost of disturbances}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\text{trace}(X_k\mathbb{E}[(x_k-\hat x_{k|k})(x_k-\hat x_{k|k})^\intercal|I_k])}_{\text{additional cost of partial information}}\]
*LQE: linear quadratic estimator, other term for the Kalman filter. \(X_k=A^\intercal P_{k+1}B(R+B^\intercal P_{k+1}B)^{-1}B^\intercal P_{k+1}A\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
23 Discussion

The separation principle also holds for the infinite horizon problem where we consider the average cost

\[\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\Big[\begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q&S\\S^\intercal&R\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k\\u_k\end{bmatrix}\Big]\]

In this case the observer is the so-called stationary Kalman filter and the control is the LQR controller with static gains.

25 Kalman filter
Given:
Dynamic model \(\ x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k+w_k\), \(x_0\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar x_0,\bar\Phi_0)\) \(\qquad\) Output equation \(\ y_k=Cx_k+n_k\), \(n_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,V)\), \(w_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,W)\)
Information set \(\ I_k=(y_0,y_1,\dots,y_k,u_0,u_1,\dots,u_{k-1})\), \(k\geq 0\)
Then: \(P_{x_k|I_k} \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat x_{k|k},\Phi_{k|k})\) is Gaussian with mean and covariance iteratively computed by:
\[\hat x_{k|k} = \hat x_{k|k-1}+L_k(y_k-C\hat x_{k|k-1}) \qquad \hat x_{k+1|k}=A\hat x_{k|k}+Bu_k\]
\[\Phi_{k|k} = \Phi_{k|k-1}-\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal(C\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal+V)^{-1}C\Phi_{k|k-1} \qquad \Phi_{k+1|k}=A\Phi_{k|k}A^\intercal+W\]
\[L_k = \Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal(C\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal+V)^{-1}\]
Initial condition: \(\hat x_{0|-1}=\bar x_0\), \(\Phi_{0|-1}=\bar\Phi_0\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
26 Justification
Why is \(P_{x_k|I_k}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat x_{k|k},\Phi_{k|k})\) Gaussian? Bayes’ rule!
Let us consider a simple example. General case is discussed in Appendix B.
Consider the initial stage, \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}\), \(y_0=x_0+n_0\), and let the a priori probability distributions be
\[f_{x_0}(x_0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_0}e^{-\frac{(x_0-\bar x_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}} \qquad f_{y_0|x_0}(y_0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_n}e^{-\frac{(y_0-x_0)^2}{2\sigma_n^2}}\]





Think of \(x_0\) as the position of a robot and \(y_0\) as a sensor measurement.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
27 Justification
Then, from Bayes’ rule
\[\text{Prob}[x_0\in A|y_0\in B] = \alpha\,\text{Prob}[y_0\in B|x_0\in A]\,\text{Prob}[x_0\in A]\]
or in terms of probability densities
\[f_{x_0|y_0}(x_0) = \alpha f_{y_0|x_0}(y_0)f_{x_0}(x_0) \qquad \alpha \text{ -- function of } \bar x_0, y_0\]
\[= \alpha\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_n}e^{-\frac{(y_0-x_0)^2}{2\sigma_n^2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_0}e^{-\frac{(x_0-\bar x_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_{0|0}}e^{-\frac{(x_0-\hat x_{0|0})^2}{2\sigma_{0|0}^2}} \quad \text{(after some calculations)}\]
also Gaussian!
\[\hat x_{0|0} = \bar x_0+L_0(y_0-\bar x_0) \qquad \sigma_{0|0}^2 = \sigma_0^2-\frac{\sigma_0^4}{\sigma_0^2+\sigma_n^2} \qquad L_0=\frac{\sigma_0^2}{\sigma_0^2+\sigma_n^2}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
28 Justification
\(P_{x_0}\), \(P_{y_0|x_0}\) (as above), and, based on the measurement \(y_0\), we update our new belief \(P_{x_0|I_0}\) on \(x_0\):





Shown for three example measurements \(y=1.2\), \(y=3\), \(y=0.5\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
29 Justification
What about \(P_{x_1|I_1}\)?

\(x_1\) is a sum of Gaussian random variables when conditioned on \(u_0,y_0\)

\[x_1 = ax_0+bu_0+w\]
and therefore \(P_{x_1|u_0,y_0}\) is Gaussian.

Apply again Bayes’ rule to prove that \(P_{x_1|I_1}\) is Gaussian.

If we continue this procedure we obtain that \(P_{x_k|I_k}\) is Gaussian for every \(k\).

33 LQG design
Given: \(\ x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k+w_k\), \(x_0\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar x_0,\bar\Phi_0)\) \(\qquad\) \(y_k=Cx_k+n_k\), \(n_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,V)\), \(w_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,W)\)
Cost function \(\quad \displaystyle\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\Big[\begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q&S\\S^\intercal&R\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k\\u_k\end{bmatrix}\Big]\)
Obtain:
Controller gains \(\quad \bar P=A^\intercal \bar PA+Q-(S+A^\intercal \bar PB)(B^\intercal \bar PB+R)^{-1}(S^\intercal+B^\intercal \bar PA) \qquad \bar K=-(B^\intercal \bar PB+R)^{-1}(S^\intercal+B^\intercal \bar PA)\)
Observer gains \(\quad \bar\Phi=A\bar\Phi A^\intercal-A\bar\Phi C^\intercal(C\bar\Phi C^\intercal+V)^{-1}C\bar\Phi A^\intercal+W \qquad \bar L=\bar\Phi C^\intercal(C\bar\Phi C^\intercal+V)^{-1}\)
LQG controller:
\[\hat x_{k+1|k}=A\hat x_{k|k}+Bu_k \qquad \hat x_{k|k}=\hat x_{k|k-1}+\bar L(y_k-C\hat x_{k|k-1}) \qquad u_k=\bar K\hat x_{k|k}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
34 Remarks

According to our convention \(u_k\) depends on \(y_k\). This means that we assume that at instant \(k\), the sensor measurement \(y_k\) is acquired, the control input is computed, and the actuation is updated.
Since there are inevitably computation delays it is common practice to make \(u_k=\bar K\hat x_{k|k-1}\) which can be computed between time steps \(k\) and \(k+1\).
In the latter case we only need to run the following equations (Luenberger observer)

\[\hat x_{k+1|k} = A\hat x_{k|k-1}+Bu_k+\tilde L(y_k-C\hat x_{k|k-1}) \qquad u_k=\bar K\hat x_{k|k-1}\]
where \(\tilde L=A\bar L\).

To use our implementation with Matlab function kalman.m used option ‘current’, and for this other implementation use ‘delayed’.
Using either implementation one can show that the closed-loop is stable due to stability of \(A+B\bar K\), \(A+\tilde LC\).
The average cost function has now the value (which can be concluded by dividing the finite horizon cost by the horizon, taking the limit as \(T\to\infty\))

\[\text{trace}(\bar PW)+\text{trace}(\bar X\bar\Phi) \qquad \bar X=A^\intercal \bar PB(R+B^\intercal \bar PB)^{-1}B^\intercal \bar PA\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
35 Inverted pendulum





Linearized model (see [1, p. 32]) \(\quad (I+m\ell^2)\ddot\theta-mg\ell\theta=m\ell\ddot x \qquad (M+m)\ddot x+b\dot x-m\ell\ddot\theta=u\)
State space
\[\frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix}x\\\dot x\\\theta\\\dot\theta\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&1&0&0\\0&-\frac{(I+m\ell^2)b}{q}&\frac{m^2g\ell^2}{q}&0\\0&0&0&1\\0&-\frac{m\ell b}{q}&\frac{mg\ell(M+m)}{q}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\\dot x\\\theta\\\dot\theta\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}0\\\frac{I+m\ell^2}{q}\\0\\\frac{m\ell}{q}\end{bmatrix}u(t) \qquad q=(I+m\ell^2)(M+m)-m^2\ell^2\]
\[y_k = \begin{bmatrix}1&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x(k\tau)\\\dot x(k\tau)\\\theta(k\tau)\\\dot\theta(k\tau)\end{bmatrix} + n_k \qquad n_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_n) \qquad \tau \text{ -- sampling period}\]
[1] Feedback control of dynamic systems, Franklin, Powell, Emani-Naeini

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
36 Time responses
\(Q=I, S=0, R=1, \tau=0.1 \qquad W=I, V=1 \qquad \sigma_n=0.0001 \qquad x_0=[1\ \ 0\ \ 0\ \ 0]^\intercal\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
37 Tuning

In practice the matrices \(V=\mathbb{E}[n_kn_k^\intercal]\), \(W=\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal]\) are used as tuning knobs to improve the state estimation.
To facilitate the tuning, these matrices are typically chosen as diagonal matrices.
If the filter is too “nervous”, i.e. it reacts very fast, and consequently the estimates are very noisy – in this case, pick weights to trust less the sensors and more the model, that is, increase \(V\) and decrease \(W\).
If it reacts too slow (although it filters out noise), it adds a delay in the control loop which is in general bad. In this case decrease \(V\) and increase \(W\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
38 Concluding remarks
Summary

We considered output feedback linear quadratic control. In this case, and assuming that the disturbances are Gaussian: use the Kalman filter to compute \(P_{x_k|I_k}\); use the optimal linear state-feedback controller (LQR infinite horizon cost); output feedback controller = LQR + LQE (separation principle).

39 Appendix A

39.1 Proof of Theorem 1

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
section: 40 Proof of linear quadratic control result
text:
40 Proof of linear quadratic control result
Let us prove by induction that the cost-to-go, at a given time step \(k\), obtained by applying the stochastic dynamic programming algorithm to the linear quadratic control problem is
\[J_k(x_k) = x_k^\intercal P_kx_k+c_k \qquad c_k = \sum_{\ell=k}^{h-1} \text{trace}(P_{\ell+1}\mathbb{E}[w_\ell w_\ell^\intercal])\]
This holds for \(k=h\) since \(J_h(x_h)=x_h^\intercal Q_hx_h\) (\(c_h=0\)).
Assuming that it holds for a given step \(k+1\), i.e., \(J_{k+1}(x_{k+1}) = x_{k+1}^\intercal P_{k+1}x_{k+1}+c_{k+1}\), we have for step \(k\)
\[J_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k} \mathbb{E}_{w_k}\big[x_k^\intercal Q_kx_k+u_k^\intercal R_ku_k+2x_k^\intercal S_ku_k+x_{k+1}^\intercal P_{k+1}x_{k+1}+c_{k+1}\,|\,x_k\big]\]
Replacing \(x_{k+1}=A_kx_k+B_ku_k+w_k\) we obtain:
\[\underbrace{J_k(x_k)}_{} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{w_k}\big[w_k^\intercal P_{k+1}(A_kx_k+B_ku_k)+(A_kx_k+B_ku_k)^\intercal P_{k+1}w_k+w_k^\intercal P_{k+1}w_k\big]+c_{k+1}}_{\text{new terms with respect to deterministic DP}}\] \[+\ \underbrace{\min_{u_k}\big[x_k^\intercal Q_kx_k+u_k^\intercal R_ku_k+2x_k^\intercal S_ku_k+(A_kx_k+B_ku_k)^\intercal P_{k+1}(A_kx_k+B_ku_k)\big]}_{\text{the same terms obtained with deterministic DP}}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
section: 41 Proof of linear quadratic control result
text:
41 Proof of linear quadratic control result
Note that the first two terms are zero since
\[\mathbb{E}_{w_k}\big[w_k^\intercal P_{k+1}(A_kx_k+B_ku_k)\big] = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{w_k}[w_k]}_{=0}^\intercal P_{k+1}(A_kx_k+B_ku_k)\]
and the third term is \(\mathbb{E}[w_k^\intercal Pw_k] = \mathbb{E}[\text{trace}(w_k^\intercal Pw_k)] = \text{trace}(P_{k+1}\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal])\).
For the same terms obtained with the deterministic DP, from the previous lecture we know that the minimisation will result in the cost \(x_k^\intercal P_kx_k\) and the control input minimiser is \(u_k=K_kx_k\).
An important conclusion is that this is also the optimal policy obtained by the stochastic DP algorithm. Then,
\[J_k(x_k) = x_k^\intercal P_kx_k + \underbrace{c_{k+1}+\text{trace}(P_{k+1}\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal])}_{c_k}\]
concluding the induction proof. The expression for the cost is then \(J_0(x_0)=x_0^\intercal P_0x_0+c_0\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
42 Appendix B

42.1 Derivation of the Kalman filter

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
43 Derivation of the Kalman filter
The following lemma, which can be found in Astrom’s book, Section 5.3, will be useful.

Lemma: If \(\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\Big(\begin{bmatrix}\bar x\\\bar y\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}R_{xx}&R_{xy}\\R_{yx}&R_{yy}\end{bmatrix}\Big)\) then \(P_{x|y}\) is Gaussian with mean \(\bar x+R_{xy}R_y^{-1}(y-\bar y)\) and covariance \(R_{xx}-R_{xy}R_{yy}^{-1}R_{yx}\).

At the initial step we have \(x_0\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat x_{0|-1},\Phi_{0|-1})\), \(y_0=Cx_0+n_0\), \(n_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,V)\). Then both \(y_0,x_0\) are Gaussian and
\[\mathbb{E}\Big[\begin{bmatrix}x_0\\y_0\end{bmatrix}\Big] = \begin{bmatrix}\hat x_{0|-1}\\C\hat x_{0|-1}\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbb{E}\Big[\begin{bmatrix}x_0-\hat x_{0|-1}\\y_0-C\hat x_{0|-1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_0-\hat x_{0|-1}\\y_0-C\hat x_{0|-1}\end{bmatrix}^\intercal\Big] = \begin{bmatrix}\Phi_{0|-1} & \Phi_{0|-1}C^\intercal \\ C\Phi_{0|-1} & C\Phi_{0|-1}C^\intercal+V\end{bmatrix}\]
Using the Lemma above, we conclude that \(P_{x_0|y_0}\) is Gaussian with mean
\[\hat x_{0|0} = \hat x_{0|-1} + \underbrace{\Phi_{0|-1}C^\intercal(C\Phi_{0|-1}C^\intercal+V)^{-1}}_{L_0}(y_0-C\hat x_{0|-1})\]
and covariance \(\quad \Phi_{0|0} = \Phi_{0|-1}-\Phi_{0|-1}C^\intercal(C\Phi_{0|-1}C^\intercal+V)^{-1}C\Phi_{0|-1}\)
Astrom’s book: Introduction to stochastic control theory, K. Astrom, 1970.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
44 Derivation of the Kalman filter
Since \(x_1=Ax_0+Bu_0+w_0\), \(x_1\) is a sum of Gaussian random variables when conditioned on \(u_0,y_0\).
Therefore \(P_{x_1|u_0,y_0}\) is Gaussian with mean
\[\hat x_{1|0} = A\hat x_{0|0}+Bu_0\]
and covariance
\[\Phi_{1|0} = A\Phi_{0|0}A^\intercal+W\]
With a similar argument to the one used in the previous slide one can conclude that \(P_{x_1|I_1}\) is Gaussian with mean \(\hat x_{1|1}\) and covariance \(\Phi_{1|1}\) and an induction argument allows to conclude the desired result.

Consider a mass spring system with unitary mass
\[\ddot y(t) = -k_sy(t)\]
\[\dot x(t) = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-\omega_n^2&0\end{bmatrix}}_{A_c}x(t) \qquad x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}y(t)\\\dot y(t)\end{bmatrix}\]
with natural period of one second (\(\omega_n=2\pi\)) and suppose that we wish to obtain an estimate of the state at a rate \(\tau=0.1\) from sensor measurements of position.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
47 Discretization
To this effect we discretize the system, obtaining
\[x_{k+1} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0.8090 & 0.0935\\-3.6932 & 0.8090\end{bmatrix}}_{A=e^{A_c\tau}}x_k + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0\\\sigma_w\end{bmatrix}}_{w_k}d_k\]
where the \(d_k\) are independent Gaussian random variables with unitary variance modeling disturbances.
The output equation is
\[y_k = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}}_{C}x_k + \underbrace{\sigma_n v_k}_{n_k} \qquad \sigma_n=0.1 \qquad \sigma_w=0.5\]
where the \(v_k\) are independent Gaussian random variables with unitary variance.
Thus, \(W=\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal]=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&\sigma_w^2\end{bmatrix} \qquad V=\mathbb{E}[n_kn_k^\intercal]=\sigma_n^2\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
48 Iterations
Assume that the covariance on the initial state \(\bar\Phi_0=\mathbb{E}[(x_0-\bar x_0)(x_0-\bar x_0)^\intercal]\) is given by
\[\Phi_{0|-1} = \bar\Phi_0 = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\]
Then we can iterate
\[\Phi_{k|k} = \Phi_{k|k-1}-\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal(C\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal+V)^{-1}C\Phi_{k|k-1}\]
\[\Phi_{k+1|k} = A\Phi_{k|k}A^\intercal+W\]
and obtain the gains \(\quad L_k = \Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal(C\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal+V)^{-1}\)

\[\Phi_{0|0} = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\Big(\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}+0.01\Big)^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0.0099&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\]

\[\Phi_{1|0} = \begin{bmatrix}0.8090&0.0935\\-3.6932&0.8090\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.0099&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.8090&0.0935\\-3.6932&0.8090\end{bmatrix}^\intercal + \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0.25\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0.0152&0.0461\\0.0461&1.0396\end{bmatrix}\]

text:
50 Iterations
For \(k=1\):
\[\Phi_{1|1} = \begin{bmatrix}0.0152&0.0461\\0.0461&1.0396\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}0.0152&0.0461\\0.0461&1.0396\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\Big(\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.0152&0.0461\\0.0461&1.0396\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}+0.01\Big)^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.0152&0.0461\\0.0461&1.0396\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0.0060&0.0183\\0.0183&0.9553\end{bmatrix}\]
\[L_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}^\intercal\!\Big/\Big(\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.0152&0.0461\\0.0461&1.0396\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}+0.01\Big) \to L_1=\begin{bmatrix}0.6037\\1.8271\end{bmatrix}\]
\[\Phi_{2|1} = \begin{bmatrix}0.8090&0.0935\\-3.6932&0.8090\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.0060&0.0183\\0.0183&0.9553\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.8090&0.0935\\-3.6932&0.8090\end{bmatrix}^\intercal + \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0.25\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0.0151&0.0599\\0.0599&0.8484\end{bmatrix}\]
For \(k=2,\dots\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
51 Expected value
Suppose that the true initial condition is \(x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and that the mean of the initial estimate is \(\hat x_{0|-1}=\bar x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.3\\0\end{bmatrix}\)
We can then iterate
\[\hat x_{k|k} = \hat x_{k|k-1}+L_k(y_k-C\hat x_{k|k-1})\]
\[\hat x_{k+1|k} = A\hat x_{k|k}\]

For an output \(y_0=1.0979\):
\[\hat x_{0|0} = \begin{bmatrix}1.3\\0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0.9901\\0\end{bmatrix}(1.0979-1.3) = \begin{bmatrix}1.0999\\0\end{bmatrix} \qquad \hat x_{1|0} = \begin{bmatrix}0.8090&0.0935\\-3.6932&0.8090\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.0999\\0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0.8899\\-4.0623\end{bmatrix}\]

\(k\in\{0,\dots,9\}\): estimated trajectory \(x_{k|k-1}\) (prediction, +) and \(x_{k|k}\) (correction, \(\times\)) versus the true state \(x_k\) (o), in the \((y,\dot y)\) plane.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
54 Iterations
Uncertainty ellipses \(\{\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{\Phi_{k|k-1}}x \mid \|x\|=1\}\) (green, prediction) and \(\{\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{\Phi_{k|k}}x\mid\|x\|=1\}\) (red, correction), for \(k=0\) and \(k=1\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
55 Appendix D

55.1 Derivation of the LQG controller

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
56 Derivation of LQG controller
Recall that we can view \(I_k\) as the state. Therefore, these are now the costs-to-go:
\[J_\ell(I_\ell) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=\ell}^{h-1} x_k^\intercal Qx_k+u_k^\intercal Ru_k+x_h^\intercal Q_hx_h\,\Big|\,I_\ell\Big]\]
when \(u_k=\mu_k(I_k)\) is the optimal policy.
Let us prove by induction that
\[J_\ell(I_\ell) = \mathbb{E}[x_\ell^\intercal P_\ell x_\ell|I_\ell]+a_\ell \qquad a_\ell = \sum_{k=\ell}^{h-1}\text{trace}(P_{k+1}W)+\sum_{k=\ell}^{h-1}\text{trace}(X_k\Phi_k)\]
This holds for \(\ell=h\) with \(a_h=0\); let us assume it holds for \(\ell+1\) and let us prove it for \(\ell\).
From the stochastic DP algorithm we have
\[J_\ell(I_\ell) = \min_{u_\ell=\mu_\ell(I_\ell)} \mathbb{E}\big[x_\ell^\intercal Qx_\ell+u_\ell^\intercal Ru_\ell+\underbrace{J_{\ell+1}(I_{\ell+1})}_{\mathbb{E}[x_{\ell+1}^\intercal P_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1}|I_{\ell+1}]+a_{\ell+1}}\,\big|\,I_{\ell+1}\big]\]
From the tower property \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[x_{\ell+1}^\intercal P_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1}|I_{\ell+1}]|I_\ell]=\mathbb{E}[x_{\ell+1}^\intercal P_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1}|I_\ell]\), therefore
\[J_\ell(I_\ell) = \min_{u_\ell=\mu_\ell(I_\ell)} \mathbb{E}\big[x_\ell^\intercal Qx_\ell+u_\ell^\intercal Ru_\ell+x_{\ell+1}^\intercal P_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1}\,\big|\,I_\ell\big]+a_{\ell+1}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
57 Derivation of LQG controller
Using similar derivations to the case of full state feedback (\(w_k\) independent of \(I_k\))
\[\mathbb{E}\big[x_\ell^\intercal(A^\intercal P_{\ell+1}A+Q)x_\ell+u_\ell^\intercal(R+B^\intercal P_{\ell+1}B)u_\ell+2u_\ell^\intercal B^\intercal P_{\ell+1}Ax_\ell\,|\,I_\ell\big] + \text{trace}\big(P_{\ell+1}\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[w_\ell w_\ell^\intercal|I_\ell]}_{W}\big)\]
Since \(u_\ell\) are constant given \(I_\ell\) the minimisation boils down to
\[\min_{u_\ell} u_\ell^\intercal(R+B^\intercal P_{\ell+1}B)u_\ell+2u_\ell^\intercal B^\intercal P_{\ell+1}A\,\mathbb{E}[x_\ell|I_\ell]\]
whose optimal solution is
\[u_\ell = -(R+B^\intercal P_{\ell+1}B)^{-1}B^\intercal P_{\ell+1}A\,\mathbb{E}[x_\ell|I_\ell]\]
Replacing this expression in the expression for the cost-to-go, and noting that \(\mathbb{E}[x_\ell|I_\ell]=x_\ell+(\mathbb{E}[x_\ell|I_\ell]-x_\ell)\), and that \(\mathbb{E}[x_\ell^\intercal Y(\mathbb{E}[x_\ell|I_\ell]-x_\ell)|I_\ell]=0\) for any \(Y\),
\[J_\ell(I_\ell) = \mathbb{E}\Big[x_\ell^\intercal\underbrace{(A^\intercal P_{\ell+1}A+Q-X_\ell)}_{P_\ell}x_\ell\,\Big|\,I_\ell\Big] + \underbrace{\text{trace}\Big(X_\ell\mathbb{E}\big[(x_\ell-\mathbb{E}[x_\ell|I_\ell])(x_\ell-\mathbb{E}[x_\ell|I_\ell])^\intercal\big]\Big)+a_{\ell+1}+\text{trace}(P_{\ell+1}W)}_{a_\ell}\]
as desired.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
58 Derivation of LQG controller
The optimal policy is
\[u_\ell = -(R+B^\intercal P_{\ell+1}B)^{-1}B^\intercal P_{\ell+1}A\,\mathbb{E}[x_\ell|I_\ell] = K_k\hat x_{k|k}\]
The optimal cost is
\[J_0(I_0) = \mathbb{E}[x_0^\intercal P_0x_0|I_0] + \sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\text{trace}(P_{k+1}\mathbb{E}[w_kw_k^\intercal]) + \sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\text{trace}\big(X_k\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[(x_k-\hat x_{k|k})(x_k-\hat x_{k|k})^\intercal|I_k]}_{\Phi_{k|k}}\big)\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
59 Appendix E

59.1 Further insights on the Kalman filter

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
60 Remarks

The Kalman filter can be divided into two steps with the following interpretation.
Prediction step

\[\hat x_{k+1|k} = A\hat x_{k|k}+Bu_k \qquad \Phi_{k+1|k} = A\Phi_{k|k}A^\intercal+W\]
Based on the previous estimate predict in open loop the state at the next step.

Correction/innovation/update step

\[\hat x_{k|k} = \hat x_{k|k-1} + \underbrace{L_k(y_k-C\hat x_{k|k-1})}_{\text{Innovation}} \qquad \Phi_{k|k} = \Phi_{k|k-1}-\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal(C\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal+V)^{-1}C\Phi_{k|k-1}\]
Based on the new measurements update the estimate.

Note that in the innovation step the covariance decreases and in the prediction step the covariance (typically) increases.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
61 Remarks

Albeit counter-intuitive, the covariance matrices do not depend on the measurements and on the control input and can be computed a priori.
(Duality) The equations to update \(\Phi_{k+1|k}\)

\[\Phi_{k+1|k} = A\Phi_{k|k-1}A^\intercal - A\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal(C\Phi_{k|k-1}C^\intercal+V)^{-1}C\Phi_{k|k-1}A^\intercal+W\]
coincide with the Riccati equations from last lecture if we replace \((A,B,Q,R) \to (A^\intercal,C^\intercal,W,V)\), \(S=0\).

In particular we know that \(\Phi_{k+1|k}\to\bar\Phi\) as \(k\to\infty\), and \(L_k\to\bar L\)

\[\bar\Phi = A\bar\Phi A^\intercal - A\bar\Phi C^\intercal(C\bar\Phi C^\intercal+V)^{-1}C\bar\Phi A^\intercal+W \qquad \bar L = \bar\Phi C^\intercal(C\bar\Phi C^\intercal+V)^{-1}\]
where \(A+\tilde LC\) is stable if \((A,C)\) observable*, \(\tilde L=A\bar L\).

Thus, the equations for the state estimator become

\[\hat x_{k+1|k} = A\hat x_{k|k} + Bu_k \qquad \hat x_{k|k} = \hat x_{k|k-1}+\bar L(y_k-C\hat x_{k|k-1})\]
*less stringent conditions for convergence can be inferred from the conditions for the dual problem (slide 34, Lec. 5).

3 Discussion

We can use the policy provided by the dynamic programming algorithm assuming no disturbances to cope with disturbances.
Is this procedure optimal in any sense? In general, no.
In fact, as we show next, in the presence of disturbances it may not even be possible to define optimal decisions, since these would depend on future realizations of disturbances.

There are two assumptions that make optimal decisions well-defined

Stochastic disturbances. If we have a stochastic characterization of disturbances we can define optimal policies as the ones that minimize the expected cost. The dynamic programming framework can be extended to provide this policy.
Worst-case disturbances. Optimal control problems with worst-case disturbances can be tackled in the framework of game theory and will not be addressed in the course.
