title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
4 Outline

Dynamic programming for stage decision problems
Linear quadratic regulator

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
5 Stage decision problems
Dynamic model
\[x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k, u_k) \qquad k \in \{0,\dots,h-1\}\]
Cost function
\[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k, u_k) + g_h(x_h)\]

State \(x_k \in X_k\) and input \(u_k \in U_k(x_k)\) live in arbitrary spaces.
If these spaces are discrete this is a discrete optimization problem.
Typically \(x_k \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and \(u_k \in \mathbb{R}^m\) for every \(k \in \{0,\dots,h-1\}\).
Goals: find an optimal path and find an optimal policy.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
6 Optimal path





Stage 0, Stage 1, \(\dots\), Stage \(h-1\), Stage \(h\).

Given an initial condition \(x_0\), a path is a set of decisions \(\{u_0, u_1, \dots, u_{h-1}\}\) such that \(u_k \in U_k(x_k)\) and \(\{(x_0,u_0),\dots,(x_{h-1},u_{h-1})\}\) satisfy the equations of the dynamic model.
A path is said to be optimal if there does not exist another path with a strictly smaller cost.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
7 Optimal policy
Policy. A policy is a set of \(h\) functions \(\pi = \{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\), \(\mu_k : X_k \to U_k\).
Optimal policy. A policy is said to be optimal if for every state \(x_\ell\) at every stage \(\ell \in \{0,\dots,h-1\}\), \(\mu_\ell(x_\ell)\) is the first action of an optimal path for the tail subproblem which considers only stages \(\{\ell,\ell+1,\dots,h\}\) with initial condition \(x_\ell\) and cost
\[\sum_{k=\ell}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,u_k) + g_h(x_h)\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
8 Dynamic programming algorithm

Start with \(J_h(x_h) = g_h(x_h)\) for every \(x_h \in X_h\) and for each decision stage, starting at the last and moving backwards, \(k \in \{h-1,h-2,\dots,0\}\), compute \(\mu_k\) and \(J_k\) from
\[J_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k \in U_k(x_k)} g_k(x_k,u_k) + J_{k+1}(f_k(x_k,u_k)) \quad \text{(DP equation)}\]
and
\[\mu_k(x_k) = u_k\]
where \(u_k\) is a minimizer in the DP equation, i.e.,
\[J_k(x_k) = g_k(x_k,\mu_k(x_k)) + J_{k+1}(f_k(x_k,\mu_k(x_k)))\]
Then \(\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\) is an optimal policy.


Theorem The policy obtained with the DP algorithm is an optimal policy (proof in the appendix).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
9 Simple integrator example
Consider the following simple example of a stage-decision problem.
Dynamic model \(\quad x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k \qquad k \in \{0,1\}\)
Cost \(\quad \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^1 x_k^2 + u_k^2 + g_2(x_2)\)
Terminal cost

Quadratic: \(g_2(x_2) = x_2^2\)
Non-quadratic: \(g_2(x_2) = e^{x_2}\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
10 Quadratic terminal cost
Step 1 \(\quad x_2 = x_1 + u_1\)
\[J_1(x_1) = \min_{u_1} g_1(x_1,u_1) + g_2(x_2) = \min_{u_1} x_1^2+u_1^2+x_2^2 = \min_{u_1} \underbrace{2(x_1^2+u_1^2+x_1u_1)}_{Q_{x_1}(u_1),\ \text{quadratic function of } u_1}\]
How to compute the minimum? Differentiate and equate to zero to find the minimizer!





\[\frac{d}{du_1}Q_{x_1}(u_1)=0 \iff 2(2u_1+x_1)=0 \iff u_1=-\frac{1}{2}x_1\]
Replacing in \(Q_{x_1}(u_1)\) we obtain the cost-to-go \(J_1(x_1) = \frac{3}{2}x_1^2\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
11 Quadratic terminal cost
Step 2 \(\quad x_1 = x_0+u_0\)
\[J_0(x_0) = \min_{u_0} g_0(x_0,u_0)+J_1(x_1) = \min_{u_0} x_0^2+u_0^2+\frac{3}{2}x_1^2 = \min_{u_0} \frac{5}{2}x_0^2+3u_0x_0+\frac{5}{2}u_0^2\]
Differentiating and equating to zero we obtain a function belonging to the optimal policy
\[u_0 = -\frac{3}{5}x_0\]
which leads to the cost-to-go
\[J_0(x_0) = \frac{8}{5}x_0^2\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
12 Optimal policy and optimal path
Optimal policy
\[u_0=-\frac{3}{5}x_0 \qquad u_1=-\frac{1}{2}x_1\]
Optimal path
\[x_0=1 \quad u_0=-\frac{3}{5} \qquad\qquad u_1=-\frac{1}{5}\] \[x_0=1 \quad x_1=\frac{2}{5} \qquad\qquad x_2=\frac{1}{5}\]
Computed by using \(x_{k+1}=x_k+u_k\), \(k \in \{0,1\}\).
Optimal cost
\[J_0(1) = \frac{8}{5}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
13 Non-quadratic terminal cost
Let us try to apply the dynamic programming algorithm considering a non-quadratic terminal cost \(g_2(x_2)=e^{x_2}\).
Step 1 \(\quad x_2=x_1+u_1\)
\[J_1(x_1) = \min_{u_1} g_1(x_1,u_1)+g_2(x_2) = \min_{u_1} x_1^2+u_1^2+e^{x_2}\]
Differentiating and equating to zero, we obtain
\[2u_1+e^{x_1+u_1}=0\]
We cannot find an analytical solution

this equation implicitly determines \(u_1\) from \(x_1\) but there is not an explicit form.
This implies that it is not easy to determine \(u_1=\mu_1(x_1)\) and move to step 2.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
14 Discussion
Linear dynamic models, quadratic cost

For these problems, we can explicitly obtain the optimal policy as shown next.

Non-linear dynamic models and/or non-quadratic cost

Very hard to apply DP and hence obtain optimal policies.
This leads to approximation techniques such as discretization.
Another class of approximation techniques will be addressed in the next lectures.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
15 Outline

Dynamic programming for stage decision problems
Linear quadratic regulator

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
16 Linear quadratic regulator
Given
Dynamic model \(\quad x_{k+1}=A_kx_k+B_ku_k \qquad k \in \{0,\dots,h-1\}\)
Cost function \(\quad \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} \begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q_k & S_k \\ S_k^\intercal & R_k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k \\ u_k\end{bmatrix} + x_h^\intercal Q_h x_h\)
Find
Optimal policy \(\quad u_k=\mu_k(x_k) \qquad k \in \{0,\dots,h-1\}\)

This is the finite-horizon linear quadratic optimal control problem in discrete-time.
The solution when \(h\) approaches infinity and the matrices in the dynamic model and cost function are time-invariant is the linear quadratic regulator.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
17 Remarks

The linear quadratic regulator is one of the celebrated results in control theory and one of the main achievements of optimal control.
Assumptions: \(Q_k, R_k\) are symmetric, \(\begin{bmatrix}Q_k & S_k \\ S_k^\intercal & R_k\end{bmatrix} \geq 0\), \(Q_h \geq 0\), \(R_k > 0\).
Model and cost are often time-invariant, i.e., \(x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q & S \\ S^\intercal & R\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k \\ u_k\end{bmatrix} + x_h^\intercal Q_h x_h\)
Cost function can result from a continuous-time problem.
However, in general the cost is specified in discrete-time and used as a tuning knob to obtain desired specifications (e.g. overshoot, etc).
We focus on the stabilization problem, i.e., driving the state to zero.
For the reference tracking problem check the notes, exercises and jupyter notebooks.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
18 Dynamic programming algorithm
Step 1 \(\quad x_h = A_{h-1}x_{h-1}+B_{h-1}u_{h-1}\)
\[J_{h-1}(x_{h-1}) = \min_{u_{h-1}} \begin{bmatrix}x_{h-1}^\intercal & u_{h-1}^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q_{h-1} & S_{h-1} \\ S_{h-1}^\intercal & R_{h-1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{h-1} \\ u_{h-1}\end{bmatrix} + \underbrace{J_h(x_h)}_{x_h^\intercal Q_h x_h}\]
terminal cost: \(J_h(A_{h-1}x_{h-1}+B_{h-1}u_{h-1}) = (A_{h-1}x_{h-1}+B_{h-1}u_{h-1})^\intercal Q_h (A_{h-1}x_{h-1}+B_{h-1}u_{h-1})\)
Then
\[J_{h-1}(x_{h-1}) = \min_{u_{h-1}} x_{h-1}^\intercal(A_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h A_{h-1}+Q_{h-1})x_{h-1}\] \[+\ 2u_{h-1}^\intercal(S_{h-1}^\intercal+B_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h A_{h-1})x_{h-1} + \underbrace{u_{h-1}^\intercal(B_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h B_{h-1}+R_{h-1})u_{h-1}}_{\text{quadratic function of } u_{h-1}}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
19 Minimizing a quadratic function in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)





\[\min_{u \in \mathbb{R}^n} J(u) \qquad J(u) = u^\intercal Xu+2u^\intercal y+z \qquad X>0\]
Unique minimizer \(\quad \nabla J(u)=0 \iff 2Xu+2y=0 \iff u=-X^{-1}y\)
Minimum \(\quad J(-X^{-1}y) = y^\intercal X^{-1}XX^{-1}y-2y^\intercal X^{-1}y+z = z-y^\intercal X^{-1}y\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
20 Dynamic Programming
Step 1 (continued)
\[J_{h-1}(x_{h-1}) = \min_{u_{h-1}} x_{h-1}^\intercal \underbrace{(A_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h A_{h-1}+Q_{h-1})}_{z} x_{h-1}\] \[+\ 2u_{h-1}^\intercal \underbrace{(S_{h-1}^\intercal+B_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h A_{h-1})}_{y} x_{h-1} + u_{h-1}^\intercal \underbrace{(B_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h B_{h-1}+R_{h-1})}_{X} u_{h-1}\]
Policy
\[u_{h-1} = -X^{-1}y = -\big(B_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h B_{h-1}+R_{h-1}\big)^{-1}\big(S_{h-1}^\intercal+B_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h A_{h-1}\big)x_{h-1}\]
Cost-to-go
\[J_{h-1}(x_{h-1}) = z-y^\intercal X^{-1}y\] \[= x_{h-1}^\intercal\Big[A_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h A_{h-1}+Q_{h-1} - (S_{h-1}+A_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h B_{h-1})(B_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h B_{h-1}+R_{h-1})^{-1}(S_{h-1}^\intercal+B_{h-1}^\intercal Q_h A_{h-1})\Big]x_{h-1}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
21 Dynamic Programming
Step 2 \(\quad x_{h-1}=A_{h-2}x_{h-2}+B_{h-2}u_{h-2}\)
\[J_{h-2}(x_{h-2}) = \min_{u_{h-2}} \begin{bmatrix}x_{h-2}^\intercal & u_{h-2}^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q_{h-2} & S_{h-2} \\ S_{h-2}^\intercal & R_{h-2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{h-2} \\ u_{h-2}\end{bmatrix} + \underbrace{J_{h-1}(x_{h-1})}_{x_{h-1}^\intercal P_{h-1} x_{h-1}}\]
Since the cost-to-go is quadratic (as the terminal cost) we can apply the same reasoning and obtain
\[u_{h-2} = K_{h-2}x_{h-2}\]
\[J_{h-2}(x_{h-2}) = x_{h-2}^\intercal P_{h-2}x_{h-2}\]
\[K_{h-2} = -\big(B_{h-2}^\intercal P_{h-1}B_{h-2}+R_{h-2}\big)^{-1}\big(S_{h-2}^\intercal+B_{h-2}^\intercal P_{h-1}A_{h-2}\big)\]
\[P_{h-2} = A_{h-2}^\intercal P_{h-1}A_{h-2}+Q_{h-2} - \big(S_{h-2}+A_{h-2}^\intercal P_{h-1}B_{h-2}\big)\big(B_{h-2}^\intercal P_{h-1}B_{h-2}+R_{h-2}\big)^{-1}\big(S_{h-2}^\intercal+B_{h-2}^\intercal P_{h-1}A_{h-2}\big)\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
22 Dynamic Programming
Step \(h-k\) \(\quad x_{k+1}=A_kx_k+B_ku_k\)
\[J_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k} \begin{bmatrix}x_k^\intercal & u_k^\intercal\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}Q_k & S_k \\ S_k^\intercal & R_k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_k \\ u_k\end{bmatrix} + \underbrace{J_{k+1}(x_{k+1})}_{x_{k+1}^\intercal P_{k+1} x_{k+1}}\]
\[u_k = K_kx_k \qquad J_k(x_k) = x_k^\intercal P_k x_k\]
\[K_k = -\big(B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k+R_k\big)^{-1}\big(S_k^\intercal+B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k\big)\]

\[P_k = A_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k+Q_k - \big(S_k+A_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k\big)\big(B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k+R_k\big)^{-1}\big(S_k^\intercal+B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k\big)\]

(Riccati equation)
Thus, simply iterate these equations for \(k \in \{h-1,\dots,1,0\}\) starting with \(P_h=Q_h\) to obtain the optimal policy \(u_k=K_kx_k\).
The optimal cost for a given initial condition is \(J_0(x_0)=x_0^\intercal P_0 x_0\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
23 Example: double integrator
Consider a double integrator





\[\ddot y(t) = \frac{F(t)}{m}\]
Continuous-time model
\[\begin{bmatrix}\dot y(t) \\ \dot v(t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}y(t) \\ v(t)\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}u(t) \qquad x(t)=[y(t)\ \ v(t)]^\intercal\]
Discretization
\[x_{k+1} = e^{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\tau}x_k + \int_0^\tau e^{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}r}dr\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}u_k = \begin{bmatrix}1 & \tau \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}x_k + \begin{bmatrix}\frac{\tau^2}{2} \\ \tau\end{bmatrix}u_k\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
24 Example: double integrator
Dynamic model \(\quad x_{k+1} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & \tau \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}x_k + \begin{bmatrix}\frac{\tau^2}{2} \\ \tau\end{bmatrix}u_k \qquad \tau=0.2\)
Qualitative goal: drive the mass to position zero in a fast way but with reasonable actuation values.
To achieve this goal let us start with this cost function
\[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} x_k^\intercal Qx_k+u_k^\intercal Ru_k+x_h^\intercal Q_hx_h\]
\[Q=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} \qquad R=1 \qquad h=5 \qquad Q_h=\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{bmatrix}\]
and then tune these parameters to improve the results.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
25 Dynamic programming
Iterate the following equations to obtain the optimal policy
\[K_k = -\big(B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k+R_k\big)^{-1}\big(S_k^\intercal+B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k\big)\]
\[P_k = A_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k+Q_k - \big(S_k+A_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k\big)\big(B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}B_k+R_k\big)^{-1}\big(S_k^\intercal+B_k^\intercal P_{k+1}A_k\big)\]
\[P_5=Q_5=\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{bmatrix} \qquad k \in \{4,3,2,1,0\}\]
First iteration
\[K_4 = -\Big(\begin{bmatrix}0.02 & 0.2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.02\\0.2\end{bmatrix}+1\Big)^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}0.02&0.2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0.2\\0&1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-0.1425 & -1.4530\end{bmatrix}\]
\[P_4 = \begin{bmatrix}1&0.2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}^\intercal\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0.2\\0&1\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}1&0.2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}^\intercal\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.02\\0.2\end{bmatrix}(-K_4) = \begin{bmatrix}10.9715 & 1.7094\\1.7094 & 8.4359\end{bmatrix}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
27 Plots and tuning
Transitory responses are still far from qualitative specifications





Guidelines to tune the cost

By increasing the terminal cost one expects that the response gets closer to the desired final position.
Same is expected by penalizing more the position error relatively to the velocity error.
Decreasing the penalty on the control action will allow more control authority to reach the origin.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
28 Increasing terminal cost
Final position error improved by increasing terminal cost

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
29 Changing state cost
Increasing position cost leads to smaller position error and larger velocity

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
30 Changing control cost
Decreasing control penalty leads to fast responses, but large actuation!

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
31 Cheap control
As \(R \to 0\) we obtain deadbeat control: zero state is achieved in 2 steps





Can we then always drive a mass to zero in two sampling periods?

No, because this typically requires very large unfeasible actuations.
Actuators have limitations which were not incorporated in our linear model.
In this LQR framework the solution is to increasingly penalize the control input until actuation constraints are met. More on this point later.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
32 Increasing the horizon
Let us increase the horizon considering \(Q=Q_h=I\), \(R=1\), \(x_0=[1\ \ 0]^\intercal\)





\(h=10\): cost \(J_0(x_0)=x_0^\intercal P_0 x_0 = 8.347\) \(\qquad\) \(h=30\): cost \(J_0(x_0)=x_0^\intercal P_0 x_0 = 9.1881\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
33 Increasing the horizon





\(h=50\): cost \(J_0(x_0)=x_0^\intercal P_0 x_0 = 9.1890\) \(\qquad\) \(h=100\): cost \(J_0(x_0)=x_0^\intercal P_0 x_0 = 9.1890\)
The cost converges to a constant as the time horizon increases.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
34 Discussion

Since the cost is positive-definite, if the horizon is large the optimal input should drive the state to zero to stop paying cost.
This explains why the cost converges as the horizon increases.

\[\sum_{k=0}^{h_0} g_k(x_k,K_ku_k) + \underbrace{\sum_{k=h_0+1}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,K_ku_k)+g_T(x_T,u_T)}_{\approx\ 0 \text{ since } x_k\approx 0 \text{ and } u_k=K_kx_k}\]

This reasoning is valid for every initial condition. Thus if \(x_0^\intercal P_0 x_0\) converges as \(h\to\infty\) then \(P_0\) converges, where \(P_0\) results from the recursion

\[P_k = A^\intercal P_{k+1}A+Q - (S+A^\intercal P_{k+1}B)(B^\intercal P_{k+1}B+R)^{-1}(S^\intercal+B^\intercal P_{k+1}A) \qquad k \in \{h-1,h-2,\dots,0\}\]

Note that we are now considering time-invariant \(A_k, B_k, Q_k, R_k, S_k\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
35 Discussion
For the double integrator example with \(Q=Q_h=I\), \(R=1\):





\(P_k=\begin{bmatrix}p_{1,k}&p_{2,k}\\p_{2,k}&p_{3,k}\end{bmatrix} \qquad K_k=\begin{bmatrix}K_{1,k}&K_{2,k}\end{bmatrix}\)
Let \(\bar P\) denote the limit \(P_0\) of the recursion; \(P_k = A^\intercal P_{k+1}A+Q-(S+A^\intercal P_{k+1}B)(B^\intercal P_{k+1}B+R)^{-1}(S^\intercal+B^\intercal P_{k+1}A)\), then \(\bar P = A^\intercal \bar P A+Q-(S+A^\intercal \bar P B)(B^\intercal \bar P B+R)^{-1}(S^\intercal+B^\intercal \bar P A)\)
Moreover, \(K_k \to \bar K\), \(\quad \bar K = -\big(B^\intercal \bar P B+R\big)^{-1}\big(S^\intercal+B^\intercal \bar P A\big)\)

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
36 Infinite horizon LQR

Proposition (special case of [Bertsekas, Sec. 4., Proposition 4.4.1]) The optimal policy for the stage decision problem with infinite number of stages with dynamic model
\[x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k \qquad (A,B) \text{ controllable}\]
and cost function
\[\sum_{k=0}^\infty x_k^\intercal Qx_k+2x_k^\intercal Su_k+u_k^\intercal Ru_k \qquad \begin{bmatrix}Q&S\\S^\intercal&R\end{bmatrix}>0\]
is given by
\[u_k=\bar K x_k \qquad \bar K = -\big(B^\intercal \bar P B+R\big)^{-1}\big(S^\intercal+B^\intercal \bar P A\big)\]
where \(\bar P\) is the unique positive definite solution to the algebraic Riccati equation

\[\bar P = A^\intercal \bar P A+Q - \big(S+A^\intercal \bar P B\big)\big(B^\intercal \bar P B+R\big)^{-1}\big(S^\intercal+B^\intercal \bar P A\big)\]

Furthermore the closed-loop \(x_{k+1}=(A+BK)x_k\) is exponentially stable.

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
37 Discussion

For simplicity, throughout the discussion, we assume \(S=0\).
As mentioned in [Bertsekas, Sec. 4.1], we can relax the assumptions \((A,B)\) is controllable and \(Q\) is positive definite.
In fact, if \((A,B)\) is controllable, \(R\) is positive definite, \(Q=NN^\intercal\) for a full rank \(N \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) (not necessarily positive definite if \(r<n\)) and \((A,N)\) is observable, then the previous theorem still holds.
Moreover, if we further relax the assumptions to \(R\) is positive definite, \((A,B)\) is stabilizable, \(N\) full rank and \((A,N)\) is detectable then the theorem still holds except that \(P\) is not necessarily positive definite.
Actually according to “Linear optimal control”, B. O. Andersson, J. B. Moore, Sec 14.1, we just need to assure that \(B^\intercal QB+R\) is positive definite and \((A,N)\) is observable to guarantee stability of the closed-loop.
Therefore, we can for instance pick \(R=0\) and \(Q\) positive definite and the closed-loop is stable (this will not be the case for continuous-time optimal control problems).

To summarize:

Stage decision problems are extensions of discrete optimization problems for which state and input spaces can be arbitrary.

42.1 Proof of optimality of dynamic programming

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
43 Proof of optimality

Theorem
The policy obtained with the DP algorithm is an optimal policy.


Proof
We shall prove using induction that \(\pi^k := \{\mu_k,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\) obtained by the DP algorithm is an optimal policy for the subproblem from stage \(k\) to stage \(h-1\) and that \(J_k(x_k)\) is the cost of the optimal path starting at \(x_k\).

Step I: Prove this for \(k=h-1\).
Step II: Assume that the induction hypothesis holds for a given \(k-1\) and prove it for \(k\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
44 Step I

By construction \(\pi^{h-1}=\{\mu_{h-1}\}\) is an optimal policy as it is the first decision of the optimal path from stage \(h-1\) to stage \(h\) since

\[\min_{u_{h-1}\in U_{h-1}(x_{h-1})} g_{h-1}(x_{h-1},u_{h-1})+J_h(f_{h-1}(x_{h-1},u_{h-1})) = g_{h-1}(x_{h-1},\mu_{h-1}(x_{h-1}))+J_h(f_{h-1}(x_{h-1},\mu_{h-1}(x_{h-1})))\]

It is also clear that

\[J_{h-1}(x_{h-1}) = \min_{u_{h-1}\in U_{h-1}(x_{h-1})} g_{h-1}(x_{h-1},u_{h-1})+J_h(f_{h-1}(x_{h-1},u_{h-1}))\]
is the optimal cost for the subproblem with initial condition \(x_{h-1}\) at stage \(h-1\).

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
45 Step II

Assume now that \(\pi^{k+1} := \{\mu_{k+1},\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\) is an optimal policy and \(J_{k+1}(x_{k+1})\) is the cost of the optimal path which starts at initial state \(x_{k+1}\). We shall prove using contradiction that \(\pi^k := \{\mu_k,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\) is an optimal policy and \(J_k(x_k)\) is the cost of an optimal path which starts at initial state \(x_k\).
Argument using contradiction: if \(\pi^k\) is not optimal then there must exist a state such that \(\mu_k(x_k)\) is not the first action \(\tilde u_k (\neq \mu_k(x_k))\) of the optimal path from stage \(k\) to stage \(h\) denoted by

\[\tilde\gamma = \{(\tilde x_k,\tilde u_k), (\tilde x_{k+1},\tilde u_{k+1}), \dots, \tilde x_h)\} \qquad \tilde x_k = x_k\]

Since we are assuming that \(\pi^{k+1} := \{\mu_{k+1},\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\) is an optimal policy we must have

\[\tilde u_{\ell+1} = \mu_{\ell+1}(\tilde x_{\ell+1}) \quad \text{for every } \ell \in \{k+1,\dots,h-2\}\]

title: 4SC000 -- Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning
text:
46 Step II

The cost of such a path is

\[\bar J = \sum_{\ell=k}^{h-1} g_\ell(\tilde x_\ell,\tilde u_\ell)+g_h(\tilde x_h) = g_k(\tilde x_k,\tilde u_k) + \sum_{\ell=k+1}^{h-1} g_\ell(\tilde x_\ell,\mu_\ell(\tilde x_\ell))+g_h(\tilde x_h) = g_k(\tilde x_k,\tilde u_k)+J_{k+1}(f(\tilde x_k,\tilde u_k))\]

However, the cost of the path which has \(\mu_k(x_k)\) as the first decision is less than or equal to the cost above (contradiction)

\[J_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k} g_k(\tilde x_k,\tilde u_k)+J_{k+1}(f(\tilde x_k,\tilde u_k)) = g_k(\tilde x_k,\mu_k(x_k))+J_{k+1}(f(\tilde x_k,\mu_k(x_k)))\] \[\leq g_k(\tilde x_k,\tilde u_k)+J_{k+1}(f(\tilde x_k,\tilde u_k)) = \bar J\]

title: Unit 2 – Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Applications
text:
1 Stochastic dynamic programming
In Unit 1, the dynamic programming algorithm was developed for deterministic problems: given a state, an action always leads to a known, predictable next state. In practice, however, the evolution of a system is often affected by disturbances that cannot be predicted in advance. This unit extends the dynamic programming algorithm to problems where such disturbances are present, assuming they can be captured by a stochastic model. It illustrates the resulting stochastic dynamic programming algorithm on several applications.

1.1 A motivating example
So far, when disturbances were mentioned at all, we used the policy provided by the dynamic programming algorithm under the assumption of no disturbances to cope with them. Is this procedure optimal in any sense? In general, no. In fact, as the following example shows, in the presence of disturbances it may not even be possible to define an optimal decision in the first place, since the best choice would depend on the future realization of the disturbance – which, by definition, is not yet known when the decision must be made.
Consider moving a robot from an initial stage \(0\) to a final stage \(h\) in minimum time, on the grid shown in Fig. 1.






Fig. 1: A robot moves across a grid from an initial stage \(0\) to a final stage \(h\), avoiding the shaded obstacle and wall cells.



We first consider a deterministic formulation, and introduce disturbances afterward. If the robot is not stuck against an obstacle or a wall, it can move up, straight, or down: moving straight from stage \(i\) to stage \(i+1\) takes \(1\) time unit, and moving diagonally takes \(\sqrt{2}\) time units. If the robot is stuck against a wall or an obstacle, only one option remains, and an additional penalty of \(c\) time units is paid every time a wall or an obstacle is hit (Fig. 2).






Fig. 2: The cost of each possible move: \(1\) for a straight move, \(\sqrt{2}\) for a diagonal move, and an extra penalty \(c\) whenever the move is forced by a wall or an obstacle.



This problem can be written in the dynamic programming framework by building a transition diagram directly from these rules (Fig. 3).






Fig. 3: The transition diagram obtained from the grid and its movement rules.



Labeling the rows of the grid \(1,\dots,n\) from bottom to top (Fig. 4), the terminal cost is \(J_h(i)=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), and, for every stage \(k\in\{h-1,h-2,\dots,1,0\}\) moving backward, the cost-to-go satisfies \[J_k(1) = \sqrt{2} + c + J_{k+1}(2), \qquad J_k(n) = \sqrt{2} + c + J_{k+1}(n-1)\] at the two boundary rows (where the robot is forced against a wall), and \[J_k(i) = \min\{1+J_{k+1}(i),\ \sqrt{2}+J_{k+1}(i+1),\ \sqrt{2}+J_{k+1}(i-1)\}\] at every other, non-obstacle row, or \[J_k(i) = 1 + c + J_{k+1}(i), \qquad i \in \{2,\dots,n-1\}\] at an obstacle row, where the robot is forced to keep moving straight through the obstacle.






Fig. 4: The same grid, with rows labeled \(1\) (bottom) to \(n\) (top), used to state the boundary rows of the dynamic programming recursion.



Fig. 5 shows this recursion worked out numerically, with penalty \(c=4\): the cost-to-go grid on the left, and the resulting optimal policy on the right, obtained by applying the three equations above at every cell and stage.






Fig. 5: A numerical instance of the deterministic robot-grid problem: cost-to-go (left) and optimal policy (right), with \(c=4\).





1.2 Introducing disturbances
Now suppose that, at the particular position \(A\) marked in Fig. 6, there might be a disturbance that pushes the robot one extra position down.






Fig. 6: The same grid, with a position \(A\) at which a disturbance may push the robot one extra position down.



Fig. 7 shows the possible outcomes at position \(A\), depending on whether the disturbance occurs (in green) or not (in blue), for each of the three possible decisions.






Fig. 7: Possible outcomes at position \(A\) (blue: no disturbance; green: disturbance) for each of the three decisions.






Table 1: Cost-to-go at position \(A\), under each decision and each possible disturbance realization.






no disturbance
disturbance




decision: “up”
\(11.4+\sqrt{2}\)
\(7.83+1\)


decision: “straight”
\(7.83+1\)
\(12.2+\sqrt{2}\)


decision: “down”
\(12.2+\sqrt{2}\)
\(11.8+\sqrt{5}\)






If the future disturbance value were known in advance, the best decision would be “up” if a disturbance were about to occur, and “straight” otherwise. But absent any further assumption on the disturbance, neither decision can be said to be optimal – the best choice depends on information that is simply not available yet. This is the sense in which no optimal decision exists at position \(A\) without further assumptions on the disturbance.


1.3 Assumptions on disturbances
Two assumptions restore a well-defined notion of optimal decision.
Under a stochastic characterization of the disturbances, an optimal policy can be defined as one that minimizes expected cost; the dynamic programming framework extends naturally to provide such a policy, as shown below. Under worst-case disturbances, instead, optimal control problems are tackled within the framework of game theory, a topic not addressed in this course.
Returning to the toy robot problem, suppose the disturbance at position \(A\) is stochastic, with \(\text{Prob}[\text{disturbance}]=0.2\) and \(\text{Prob}[\text{no disturbance}]=0.8\). Weighting each outcome in Table 1 by its probability gives an expected cost for each decision:



Table 2: Expected cost-to-go at position \(A\).












no disturbance
disturbance

decision: “up”
\(11.4+\sqrt{2}\)
\(7.83+1\)
\((11.4+\sqrt{2})0.8+(7.83+1)0.2=12.02\)

\(7.83+1\)
\(12.2+\sqrt{2}\)
\((7.83+1)0.8+(12.2+\sqrt{2})0.2=9.79\)


decision: “down”
\(12.2+\sqrt{2}\)
\(11.8+\sqrt{5}\)
\((12.2+\sqrt{2})0.8+(11.8+\sqrt{5})0.2=13.69\)






The optimal decision is now well-defined: pick “straight,” which minimizes the expected cost.
Alternatively, weighting each outcome by its worst case rather than its probability gives:



Table 3: Worst-case cost-to-go at position \(A\).

Here too the optimal decision is well-defined: pick “up,” the safe choice that guarantees a cost of at most \(11.4+\sqrt{2}\) no matter what the disturbance turns out to be.


1.4 The stochastic optimal control problem
Under a stochastic characterization of disturbances, the dynamic model and cost take the form \[x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k, u_k, w_k), \qquad \sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k, u_k, w_k) + g_h(x_h),\] where the state and action still live in the same finite spaces as before, and the disturbance belongs to a finite set \(w_k \in W_k(i,j) := \{1,\dots,\omega_{i,j,k}\}\) whenever \(x_k=i\) and \(u_k=j\), characterized by the probabilities \[p_\ell^{k,i,j} := \text{Prob}[w_k = \ell \mid x_k=i,\, u_k=j], \qquad \ell \in W_k(i,j).\] Both the state and the cost are now random variables. This model is commonly referred to as a Markov Decision Process (MDP).
Given a policy \(\pi=\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\), with \(u_k=\mu_k(x_k)\), so that \(x_{k+1}=f_k(x_k,\mu_k(x_k),w_k)\), define the expected cost \[J_\pi(x_0) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,\mu_k(x_k),w_k) + g_h(x_h)\Big],\] a real number for each initial condition \(x_0\). The goal is to find a policy that minimizes \(J_\pi\).


1.5 The stochastic dynamic programming algorithm
The dynamic programming algorithm extends to this stochastic setting as follows. Initialize \(J_h(i)=g_h(i)\) for every state \(i\), and then, for each decision stage starting from the last and moving backward, \(k\in\{h-1,h-2,\dots,0\}\), compute \[J_k(i) = \min_{j \in U_k(i)} \sum_{\ell \in W_k(i,j)} p_\ell^{k,i,j} \Big(g_k(i,j,\ell) + J_{k+1}\big(f_k(i,j,\ell)\big)\Big),\] together with \(\mu_k(i)=j\), where \(j\) is a minimizer above. Then \(\{\mu_0,\dots,\mu_{h-1}\}\) is an optimal policy. Equivalently, the same recursion can be written as \[J_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k \in U_k(x_k)} \; \mathbb{E}_{w_k}\Big[g_k(x_k,u_k,w_k) + J_{k+1}\big(f_k(x_k,u_k,w_k)\big)\Big].\]
Each function \(J_\ell(i)\) is now the expected cost-to-go when \(x_\ell=i\), \[J_\ell(i) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=\ell}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,\mu_k(x_k),w_k) + g_h(x_h)\Big],\] often also written as \(J_\ell(i) = \mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{k=\ell}^{h-1} g_k(x_k,\mu_k(x_k),w_k) + g_h(x_h) \mid x_\ell=i\big]\); in particular, \(J_0(i)\) is the expected optimal cost for initial condition \(x_0=i\).


1.6 The Markov property
The name “Markov Decision Process” comes from the fact that the dynamic model has the so-called Markov property: intuitively, the probability that the process moves to a new state depends only on the current state and action, and, given these, the next state is conditionally independent of all previous states and actions. Formally, for any function \(f\), \[\mathbb{E}[f(x_{k+1}) \mid x_k, u_k, x_{k-1}, u_{k-1}, \dots, x_0, u_0] = \mathbb{E}[f(x_{k+1}) \mid x_k, u_k],\] a property that follows directly from the definition of the dynamic model above.


1.7 A stochastic version of the robot-grid example
Return to the deterministic robot-grid problem introduced earlier (Fig. 8), but now suppose that, at every regular (non-obstacle) state and stage, the evolution of the state is stochastic.






Fig. 8: The same robot-grid problem as before, now with stochastic transitions at every regular state and stage.



Fig. 9 shows the resulting transition probabilities: attempting to move up succeeds with probability \(1-2p\), but results in a straight move with probability \(2p\); attempting to move straight succeeds with probability \(1-2p\), but results in a move up or down, each with probability \(p\); and attempting to move down succeeds with probability \(1-2p\), but results in a straight move with probability \(2p\).






Fig. 9: Transition probabilities for the three actions (up, straight, down) in the stochastic robot-grid example.



The boundary and obstacle equations are unaffected by the disturbance (a wall or obstacle still forces the same move, deterministically, as in Fig. 8): \[J_k(1) = \sqrt{2}+c+J_{k+1}(2), \qquad J_k(n) = \sqrt{2}+c+J_{k+1}(n-1), \qquad J_h(i)=0,\] \[J_k(i) = 1+c+J_{k+1}(i), \qquad \text{(obstacle)}, \; i \in \{2,\dots,n-1\},\] but at every other state the cost-to-go now averages over the three possible outcomes of each action: \[
\begin{aligned}
J_k(i) = \min\Big\{\ &(1-2p)\big(1+J_{k+1}(i)\big) + p\big(\sqrt{2}+J_{k+1}(i+1)\big) + p\big(\sqrt{2}+J_{k+1}(i-1)\big), \\
&2p\big(1+J_{k+1}(i)\big) + (1-2p)\big(\sqrt{2}+J_{k+1}(i+1)\big), \\
&2p\big(1+J_{k+1}(i)\big) + (1-2p)\big(\sqrt{2}+J_{k+1}(i-1)\big)\ \Big\}, \qquad i \in \{2,\dots,n-1\},
\end{aligned}
\] matching, term by term, the “straight,” “up,” and “down” actions of Fig. 9. Compare with the deterministic recursion obtained earlier for the same non-obstacle rows, \(J_k(i) = \min\{1+J_{k+1}(i),\ \sqrt{2}+J_{k+1}(i+1),\ \sqrt{2}+J_{k+1}(i-1)\}\): as \(p\to 0\), the stochastic recursion reduces exactly to the deterministic one.











(a) Cost-to-go











(b) Optimal policy







Fig. 10: A numerical instance of the stochastic robot-grid problem, with \(p=0.1\) and \(c=4\): cost-to-go (a) and optimal policy (b).



The resulting optimal policy, compared with the deterministic one obtained earlier for the same grid, is quite intuitive: it steers well clear of the obstacles rather than hugging them closely, since a move adjacent to an obstacle now carries some probability of being pushed into it (Fig. 11).






Fig. 11: Comparing the deterministic policy (left), which hugs the obstacles, with the stochastic policy (right), which keeps a wider safety margin around them.





1.8 Coping with disturbances in practice
Three strategies can be followed once disturbances are present. The first, open loop, applies the control inputs of a single precomputed optimal path and ignores any disturbance realized along the way; this may not make sense at all, and can lead to poor performance or even instability. The second follows the feedback policy obtained from the deterministic dynamic programming algorithm, simply neglecting disturbances; this is often the strategy followed in practice, especially in engineering contexts, owing to the difficulty of obtaining a reliable stochastic characterization of the disturbances – later in the course this will be called certainty-equivalent control. The third follows the feedback policy obtained from the dynamic programming algorithm for the full stochastic model; this is important in operations research problems, games, and similar settings, but sees more limited use in practical control applications, again because a stochastic model of the disturbances is often hard to obtain.
The three strategies can be compared numerically on the same robot-grid instance and the same disturbance realizations.
Under the open-loop strategy, the optimal decisions are first computed for a given initial state assuming no disturbances (predicted cost \(13.8\)), and then blindly applied regardless of what actually happens: the perturbed path shown in Fig. 12 has a realized cost of \(26.66\), and the average cost over \(1000\) perturbed paths is \(22.04\) (open-loop decisions are applied only at regular cells; at obstacle and wall cells the option is unique regardless).











(a) Policy











(b) Realized path







Fig. 12: Open-loop strategy: the precomputed policy (a, with the planned path highlighted) and the actually realized path under disturbances (b), which drifts into cells the plan did not anticipate.



Under the closed-loop, deterministic-DP strategy, the optimal policy assuming no disturbances is computed once, but the decision is re-made online at every stage based on the state actually observed: the perturbed path in Fig. 13 has a realized cost of \(19.07\), and the average cost over \(1000\) perturbed paths is \(17.51\) – already a marked improvement over open loop.











(a) Policy











(b) Realized path







Fig. 13: Closed-loop strategy using the deterministic policy, re-decided online: policy (a) and realized path (b).



Finally, under the closed-loop, stochastic-DP strategy, the optimal policy accounting for disturbances is computed once, and again re-decided online at every stage: the perturbed path in Fig. 14 has a realized cost of \(15.48\), and the average cost over \(1000\) perturbed paths is \(15.96\) – the best of the three strategies.











(a) Policy











(b) Realized path







Fig. 14: Closed-loop strategy using the stochastic policy, re-decided online: policy (a) and realized path (b).





1.9 An equivalent formulation using transition probabilities
It is often more convenient to specify the dynamic model \(x_{k+1}=f_k(x_k,u_k,w_k)\) directly in terms of transition probabilities, \[[P_k(j)]_{ri} = \text{Prob}[x_{k+1}=r \mid x_k=i,\, u_k=j],\] rather than through an explicit function \(f_k\) and disturbance \(w_k\). For example, suppose \[x_{k+1} = \min\{\max\{x_k+u_k+w_k,\,1\},\,c_k\}, \qquad c_k = \begin{cases}2 & k \text{ odd}\\3 & k \text{ even}\end{cases},\] with \(u_k\in\{1,2\}\), \(\text{Prob}[w_k=0]=2/3\), and \(\text{Prob}[w_k=-1]=1/3\). Then, for odd \(k\), \[P_k(1) = \begin{bmatrix}1/3 & 1\\2/3 & 0\end{bmatrix}, \qquad P_k(2) = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix},\] and for even \(k\), \[P_k(1) = \begin{bmatrix}1/3 & 0 & 0\\2/3 & 1/3 & 0\\0 & 2/3 & 1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad P_k(2) = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 0\\1/3 & 0 & 0\\2/3 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\]
Conversely, given a set of transition probabilities, a trivial dynamic model reproducing them can always be constructed by taking \(w_k\) to be the next state itself, \(x_{k+1}=w_k\), with \(\text{Prob}[w_k=j \mid x_k=i,\, u_k=\ell] = P_{ji}(\ell)\). If the running cost depends only on state and action it is unchanged; if it also depends on the disturbance, it is replaced by \[\sum_{k=0}^{h-1} \mathbb{E}\big[g_k(x_k,u_k,w_k)+g_h(x_h)\big] \;\longrightarrow\; \sum_{k=0}^{h-1} \mathbb{E}\big[\tilde{g}(x_k,u_k)+g_h(x_h)\big], \qquad \tilde{g}(i,u) = \sum_j P_{ji}(u)\, g_k(i,u,j).\] In this formulation, the dynamic programming equations read \[J_k(i) = \min_u \; \tilde{g}(i,u) + \sum_j P_{ji}(u) J_{k+1}(j), \qquad J_h(i) = g_h(i),\] for every state \(i\).






NoteStochastic dynamic programming for the inventory control example, revisited





The stochastic dynamic programming algorithm can be applied to the inventory control example of Unit 1, now with uncertain demand at stage \(2\): \(\text{Prob}[d_2=0]=0.5\), \(\text{Prob}[d_2=1]=0.5\). Fig. 15 shows the resulting cost-to-go and decisions across all four stages.






Fig. 15: The inventory control example revisited with a stochastic demand at stage 2.



Since there is only a single disturbance realization affecting stage \(2\)’s transitions, the costs-to-go at stage \(3\) coincide with those already obtained in the deterministic case of Unit 1. The decisions at stage \(2\) are the ones minimizing the expected cost-to-go: for state \(0\), decision \(u_2=1\) is better than \(u_2=2\), and is in fact optimal. Fig. 16 works out, for state \(x_2=2\), the expected cost-to-go under each of the three possible decisions.






Fig. 16: Computing the expected cost-to-go at state \(x_2=2\) under each of the three possible decisions.



At stages \(0\) and \(1\) there is no uncertainty, so the corresponding costs-to-go are obtained by applying the ordinary dynamic programming algorithm, using the expected costs-to-go already computed at stage \(2\) as the terminal values for that part of the recursion.

title: Unit 2 – Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Applications
text:
2 Applications
Stochastic dynamic programming has a large number of applications in management, finance, games, operations research, and other areas requiring decisions under uncertainty. This section focuses on two of them: optimal stopping problems, where at every stage one must decide either to stop or to continue a given process, possibly at a cost – one of the simplest applications of the framework – and planning under uncertainty, illustrated by the problem of spending a day at Efteling.

2.1 The car parking problem
Juliet is taking her boyfriend Romeo to watch a movie at a crowded local cinema. They are running late and need to find a parking place (Fig. 17). If they park \(k\in\{1,\dots,h\}\) places away from the cinema, they lose \(ck\) minutes of the movie; each parking place is free with probability \(p_k=1-\alpha^k\), for some \(0<\alpha<1\); and if they reach the cinema without having parked, they must wait in the cinema’s parking queue, which typically takes about \(C\) minutes. When should they park – that is, stop searching – so as to minimize their expected delay?






Fig. 17: Juliet and Romeo drive down a row of parking places, some free and some occupied, looking for a spot near the cinema.



Let \(h\) be the number of parking places, with stage \(\ell\in\{0,1,\dots,h-1\}\) corresponding to distance \(k=h-\ell\) from the cinema. The state \(x_\ell\in\{F,S,O\}\) records whether parking spot \(\ell\) is free (\(F\)), occupied (\(O\)), or the car is already parked (\(S\)), with terminal state \(x_h=E\). When \(x_\ell=F\), the action is \(u\in\{P,DP\}\): park (\(P\), cost \(ck\)) or don’t park (\(DP\), cost \(0\)); when \(x_\ell=O\), the only available action is \(u_\ell=DP\). If \(u_\ell=DP\), then \(x_{\ell+1}=F\) with probability \(1-\alpha^{h-(\ell+1)}\) and \(x_{\ell+1}=O\) with probability \(\alpha^{h-(\ell+1)}\). If the decision is still not to park at the very last stage, a cost of \(C\) is incurred instead. Fig. 18 shows the resulting transition diagram.






Fig. 18: Transition diagram for the car parking problem: states \(F\) (free), \(O\) (occupied), and \(S\) (already parked), with terminal state \(E\).



Writing \(p_k=1-\alpha^k\) and \(q_k=\alpha^k\), the dynamic programming recursion is worked out stage by stage, starting from \(J_h(E)=0\) and \(J_{h-1}(O)=C\), \(J_{h-1}(F)=\min\{C,c\}\), then \[J_{h-2}(O) = p_1 J_{h-1}(F) + q_1 J_{h-1}(O) = p_1\min\{C,c\}+q_1 C, \qquad J_{h-2}(F) = \min\{p_1 J_{h-1}(F) + q_1 J_{h-1}(O),\, 2c\},\] and, in general, at stage \(h-(k+1)\), \[J_{h-(k+1)}(O) = p_k J_{h-k}(F) + q_k J_{h-k}(O), \qquad J_{h-(k+1)}(F) = \min\{p_k J_{h-k}(F) + q_k J_{h-k}(O),\, c(k+1)\}.\]
Fig. 19 works out a numerical instance with \(\alpha=0.8\), \(h=4\), \(C=3\), \(c=1\). The resulting rule is simple and intuitive: park if there is a free parking place at distance one or two from the cinema, and otherwise keep searching.






Fig. 19: A numerical instance of the car parking problem, with \(\alpha=0.8\), \(h=4\), \(C=3\), \(c=1\).









NoteAnother stopping-time problem: selling an asset





A closely related stopping-time problem is deciding when to accept an offer for an asset – a house, say – so as to maximize the expected revenue at the end of a fixed horizon (Fig. 20).






Fig. 20: When should an offer for a house be accepted, so as to maximize the expected revenue?



Suppose independent offers \(w_0,w_1,\dots,w_{N-1}\) arrive over \(N\) periods, taking values in a finite set \(w_k\in\{a_1,\dots,a_M\}\) with \(\text{Prob}[w_k=a_i]=p_i\) (\(w_k=0\) models the case of no offer in period \(k\)); that an accepted offer is invested at rate \(r\) until period \(N\); and that rejected offers are not renewed, while the last offer \(w_{N-1}\) must be accepted if nothing has been accepted before.
Let \(x_k\), for \(k\geq 1\), be the most recent offer \(w_{k-1}\), with a terminal state \(x_k=T\) once the asset has been sold, let \(u_k=1\) denote accepting offer \(w_{k-1}\) at time \(k\geq 1\), and set \(x_0:=0\). Then \[x_{k+1} = \begin{cases}T & \text{if } x_k=T,\ \text{or } x_k\neq T \text{ and } u_k=1 \text{ (sell)},\\w_k & \text{otherwise},\end{cases}\] and the expected selling price is \[\mathbb{E}_{w_k}\Big[g_N(x_N) + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_k(x_k,u_k,w_k)\Big],\] with \[g_k(x_k,u_k,w_k) = \begin{cases}(1+r)^{N-k}x_k & \text{if } x_k\neq T \text{ and } u_k=1 \text{ (sell)}\\0 & \text{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad g_N(x_N) = \begin{cases}x_N & \text{if } x_N\neq T\\0 & \text{if } x_N=T.\end{cases}\]
Applying the dynamic programming algorithm, \[J_N(x_N) = \begin{cases}x_N & \text{if } x_N\neq T\\0 & \text{if } x_N=T,\end{cases} \qquad J_k(x_k) = \begin{cases}\max\big[(1+r)^{N-k}x_k,\ \mathbb{E}[J_{k+1}(w_k)]\big] & \text{if } x_k\neq T\\0 & \text{if } x_k=T,\end{cases}\] which translates into a threshold policy: accept the offer \(x_k\) if \(x_k>\alpha_k\), and reject it if \(x_k\leq\alpha_k\), where \[\alpha_k = \mathbb{E}[J_{k+1}(w_k)] = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^M p_i J_{k+1}(a_i)}{(1+r)^{N-k}}.\]





2.2 Planning a day at Efteling
A different flavor of application is planning under uncertainty: how should an afternoon at the Efteling amusement park be planned so as to maximize the additive reward collected from one’s favorite attractions, given a stochastic model of the queueing times (Fig. 21)?






Fig. 21: Map of Efteling, with \(10\) numbered attractions plus the entrance/exit, and Duarte’s own preference rating for each attraction.



The visit is planned over the period from 14:00 to 19:00, divided into \(T=60\) time slots of \(5\) minutes each, from \(k=1\) (14:00-14:05) to \(k=T=60\) (18:55-19:00). The walking time between any two attractions – and to and from the entrance/exit, treated as an \(11\)th location – is deterministic and given in Fig. 22; a visitor never wishes to visit the same attraction more than once.






Fig. 22: Walking time, in minutes, between every pair of attractions and the entrance/exit.



Suppose the waiting-time distribution at each attraction is known as a function of time of day (Fig. 23). The state is then taken to be a triple: a unique label \(a_M a_{M-1}\cdots a_2 a_1\), with \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\), recording which attractions have been visited so far; the current time index; and the last attraction visited, \(c\in\{1,\dots,M\}\) (with \(a_c=1\)). The goal is a policy that, for every state, prescribes the next attraction to visit.






Fig. 23: Stochastic waiting-time distribution at each attraction, as a function of time of day.



Since the true horizon (closing time) is fixed but a visitor may finish their round of attractions earlier, it is convenient to consider a large number of decision stages \(T\) and define the terminal cost as \(g_T(x_T)=\infty\) if the terminal state is infeasible, and \(g_T(x_T)=0\) if it is feasible, where a state is feasible whenever, given the last attraction visited and the current time, there is still enough time left to exit the park (Fig. 24); intuitively, at the terminal stage \(T\) a visitor is assumed to exit the park even if time remains.






Fig. 24: At the terminal stage, only states from which the visitor can still reach the exit in time are feasible (cost \(0\)); all others are infeasible (cost \(\infty\)).



Fig. 25 illustrates one step of the resulting transition diagram: from a given state, the possible actions are to visit any not-yet-visited attraction, each leading to a new state at the next time index, with an arrow cost equal to minus the reward of the attraction just visited (since the framework minimizes cost, while the visitor’s true objective is to maximize reward). Writing \(c_i\) for the time to walk to attraction \(i\) plus the random waiting time once there, the new time index simply advances by the number of \(5\)-minute slots corresponding to \(c_i\).






Fig. 25: One step of the transition diagram: from a state recording the attractions visited so far, the time, and the last attraction visited, each action leads to a new state, with cost equal to minus the reward of the attraction visited.



After setting up the problem in this way, running the dynamic programming algorithm produces the optimal policy – provided the horizon \(T\) is taken long enough, in which case both the costs-to-go and the policy can be shown to converge (a fact justified later in the course). For instance, from the state \((1111100000,\, 25,\, 2)\), the optimal policy might prescribe moving next to attraction \(10\).


2.3 Other applications
Stochastic dynamic programming has also been used in student projects supervised at TU/e. Autonomous Parking Spot Ranking, by Jeroen Vanhegelsom (2022), was developed at the company Lightyear in Eindhoven, and uses stochastic dynamic programming to plan dynamic parking strategies for solar-powered cars so as to optimize their sun exposure. Optimal planning strategies balancing sensing and acting under uncertainty and partial observability, by Femke Voogt (2026), was developed at the company VBTI in Eindhoven, and uses stochastic dynamic programming to plan leaf harvesting.






NoteA simple coin-tossing game





Two players, \(A\) and \(B\), repeatedly play two fair games. Player \(A\) tosses a coin worth \(1\) money unit: on “heads” he gains \(1\) point (and \(B\) loses \(1\) point), otherwise he loses \(1\) point (and \(B\) gains \(1\) point). Alternatively, player \(A\) tosses a coin worth \(2\) money units, gaining or losing \(2\) points on the same terms. The game ends as soon as one of the players reaches \(L\) or \(L+1\) points, in which case that player receives \(L\) money units from the other; if neither player reaches \(L\) points within \(h\) stages, the game ends with no payment. Suppose \(h=2\), \(L=3\), and both players start with zero points. Can player \(A\) gain money in expectation by choosing, at each stage, which coin to toss?
Let the dynamic model be \(x_{k+1}=f(x_k,u_k,w_k)\), where \(x_k\) is player \(A\)’s point total, \(u_k\in\{1,2\}\) is the coin chosen, and \(w_k\in\{-1,1\}\) encodes tails (\(-1\)) or heads (\(1\)), for \(k\in\{0,\dots,h-1\}\): \[
f(x_k,u_k,w_k) = \begin{cases}
x_k+1 & u_k=1,\ w_k=1\\
x_k+2 & u_k=2,\ w_k=1\\
x_k-1 & u_k=1,\ w_k=-1\\
x_k-2 & u_k=2,\ w_k=-1\\
x_k & x_k \in \{L,L+1,-L,-(L+1)\} \text{ (game already over, wait for the last stage)}.
\end{cases}
\] With cost \(\min \sum_{k=0}^{h-1} g(x_k,u_k) + g_h(x_h)\), where \(g(x_k,u_k)=0\) for every \(x_k,u_k\) and \[g_h(x_h) = \begin{cases}-L & x_h=L \text{ or } x_h=L+1\\L & x_h=-L \text{ or } x_h=-(L+1)\\0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}\] (so that profit equals minus cost), the dynamic programming algorithm gives \(J_h(x_h)=g_h(x_h)\) and, for \(k\in\{h-1,\dots,0\}\), \[J_k(x_k) = \min_{u_k} \mathbb{E}\big[g(x_k,u_k) + J_{k+1}(x_{k+1}) \mid x_k\big],\] which, using the expression for \(f\) above, becomes \[
J_k(x_k) = \begin{cases}
\min\Big\{\dfrac{J_{k+1}(x_k+1)+J_{k+1}(x_k-1)}{2},\ \dfrac{J_{k+1}(x_k+2)+J_{k+1}(x_k-2)}{2}\Big\} & \text{otherwise}\\[4pt]
J_{k+1}(x_k) & x_k \in \{-(L+1),-L,L,L+1\}.
\end{cases}
\]
Iterating this recursion produces the costs-to-go and optimal decisions shown in Fig. 26 (circles are states, labeled with the number of points at a given stage; the cost-to-go is shown above each circle, and the optimal decision next to it). For the zero initial condition, the optimal expected cost is \(-3/4\), so player \(A\)’s expected profit is \(3/4\): yes, a suitably chosen coin-tossing strategy lets player \(A\) profit in expectation.






Fig. 26: Costs-to-go and optimal decisions for the coin-tossing game, with \(h=2\) and \(L=3\).

title: Unit 2 – Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Applications
text:
3 Summary
This unit extended the dynamic programming algorithm to problems affected by disturbances. We saw that, without further assumptions, an optimal decision may not even be well-defined in the presence of disturbances, and that a stochastic characterization of the disturbances restores a well-defined notion of optimality, based on minimizing expected cost. We introduced the resulting stochastic dynamic programming algorithm, together with an equivalent formulation based directly on transition probabilities rather than an explicit disturbance model. Two classes of applications illustrated the framework: optimal stopping problems – the car parking problem and, in the appendix, selling an asset – and planning under uncertainty, illustrated by spending a day at Efteling. If a stochastic characterization of the disturbances is available, it can improve, in terms of expected cost, both open-loop policies and the closed-loop policy obtained by dynamic programming under a deterministic assumption.
